<!-- theorem-1: body_md -->
Let $X=G/H$ be a reductive symmetric space. The subset 
 $\mathrm{supp}(\lambda_X)$ of $\widehat G$ is the closure of $S_X$ in the Fell topology.
<!-- end theorem-1 -->
<!-- proposition-1: body_md -->
Let \(X=G/H\) be a reductive symmetric space.
Then \(S_X\) is a closed subset of \(\widehat G\). Consequently,
\[
\mathrm{supp}(\lambda_X)=S_X. 
\]
In other words, for any irreducible unitary representation \(\pi\) of \(G\),
\(\pi\) belongs to \(\mathrm{supp}(\lambda_{X})\) if and only if there exist a
cuspidal \(\sigma\)-parabolic subgroup \(P=MAN\) of \(G\), a representation
\(\xi \in {\hat{M}}_{M\cap H, \mathrm{ds}}\) in the discrete series of
\(M/(M\cap H)\), and \(\nu \in i\mathfrak{a}_\mathfrak{q}^*\), such that \(\pi\) is equivalent to an
irreducible constituent of the generalized \(\sigma\)-principal series
representation \(\pi_{P, \xi, \nu}\).
<!-- end proposition-1 -->
<!-- theorem-2: body_md -->
Let \(X=G/H\) be a well-tempered symmetric space. Suppose that \(G\) is a
real algebraic reductive linear group with abelian Cartan subgroups and that \(X\) has discrete
series. For an irreducible unitary representation \((\pi,V)\) of \(G\), the
following conditions are equivalent:
\begin{enumerate}[(1)]
\item \(\pi\) belongs to the discrete series of the symmetric space~$X$; 
\item \(\pi\) is tempiric with regular infinitesimal character, and its unique
lowest \(K\)-type \(\tau_\pi\) has nonzero $(K \cap H)$-fixed vectors; 
\item \(\pi\) is irreducibly induced from a discrete character datum $(TA, \Gamma, \lambda, 0)$ (see Definition~\ref{def:dataC})  based on the fundamental Cartan subgroup
\(TA=Z_G(\mathfrak{l})\), where \(\lambda\in i\mathfrak{t}_\mathfrak{q}^\ast\) is \(G\)-regular and $
\Gamma|_{T\cap H}=1$.
\end{enumerate}
Moreover, for any \((\pi,V)\) satisfying these equivalent conditions, the space of square-integrable $H$-invariant distribution vectors of~$\pi$ is isomorphic with the space of $(K\cap H)$-invariant vectors of~$\tau_\pi$. In particular,
\[
\dim_\mathbb{C} (V^{-\infty})^H_{\mathrm{ds}}
=
\dim_\mathbb{C} \tau_\pi^{K\cap H}.
\]
<!-- end theorem-2 -->
<!-- theorem-3: body_md -->
Let \(X=G/H\) be a well-tempered symmetric space, and suppose that \(G\) is
a real reductive linear group in Vogan's class. Let \(\pi\in\widehat G\) be an
irreducible unitary representation of \(G\). Then \(\pi\) belongs to
\(\operatorname{supp}(\lambda_X)\) if and only if \(\pi\) is equivalent to an
irreducible constituent of \(X_G(TA,\Gamma,\lambda,\nu)\) for some character
datum \((TA,\Gamma,\lambda,\nu)\) for \(X\).
<!-- end theorem-3 -->
<!-- theorem-4: body_md -->
\label{thm-shape-intro}
Let \(X=G/H\) be a well-tempered symmetric space, where $G$ is a linear reductive group with abelian Cartan subgroups.   Then 
\[
\operatorname{supp}(\lambda_X)_{\mathrm{Haus}}
=
\bigsqcup_{c\in\mathcal C_X}\Sigma_X(c).
\]
<!-- end theorem-4 -->
<!-- theorem-5: body_md -->
\label{thm-gc-gr-intro}
Let \(X=G/H\) be a symmetric space of type \(G_{\mathbb C}/G_{\mathbb R}\).
Then:
\begin{enumerate}[(1)]
\item \(X\) is well-tempered.

\item For every \(\theta\)-stable Cartan subalgebra
\(\mathfrak{b}_\mathfrak{h}=\mathfrak{t}_\mathfrak{h}\oplus\mathfrak{a}_\mathfrak{h}\subset\mathfrak{h}\), and for every discrete character datum
\((TA,\Gamma,\lambda)\) for \(X\) based on
\(TA=Z_G(\mathfrak{b}_\mathfrak{h}\oplus i\mathfrak{b}_\mathfrak{h})\), the map
\[
 i\mathfrak{a}_\mathfrak{q}^\ast/W^\sigma(\lambda)
 \longrightarrow \widehat G_{\mathrm{temp}},
 \qquad
 \overline\nu\longmapsto X_G(TA,\Gamma,\lambda,\nu),
\]
is a homeomorphism onto its image.  Denote this image by
$\widehat X_{\mathfrak{b}_\mathfrak{h},\lambda}$; then
\[
\mathrm{supp}(\lambda_X)
=
\bigsqcup_{[\mathfrak{b}_\mathfrak{h}]}
\ \bigsqcup_{[(\Gamma,\lambda)]}
\widehat X_{\mathfrak{b}_\mathfrak{h},\lambda},
\]
where \([\mathfrak{b}_\mathfrak{h}]\) runs over the \(K\)-conjugacy classes of \(\theta\)-stable
Cartan subalgebras of \(\mathfrak{h}\), and \([(\Gamma,\lambda)]\) runs over the
\(W^\sigma(\mathfrak{b}_\mathfrak{h})\)-orbits of discrete character data for \(X\) based on
\(TA=Z_G(\mathfrak{b}_\mathfrak{h}\oplus i\mathfrak{b}_\mathfrak{h})\).

\item \(X\) has discrete series if and only if the real Lie algebra \(\mathfrak{h}\) is
split.  In that case the discrete series of \(X\) is precisely the set of
representations
\[
X_G(TA,\Gamma,\lambda,0)
\]
attached to split Cartan subalgebras of \(\mathfrak{h}\) and to the corresponding
discrete character data for \(X\).  Equivalently, it is the set of tempiric
representations of \(G\) with regular infinitesimal character whose unique
lowest \(K\)-type is \(K\cap H\)-spherical.

\item A representation in \(\mathrm{supp}(\lambda_X)\) belongs to the discrete series
of \(X\) if and only if it is an isolated point of \(\mathrm{supp}(\lambda_X)\).
\end{enumerate}
<!-- end theorem-5 -->
<!-- corollary-1: body_md -->
With the notation of Theorem~\ref{thm-gc-gr-intro}, there is a canonical
isomorphism
\[
C^*_{\lambda_X}(G)
\cong
\bigoplus_{[\mathfrak{b}_\mathfrak{h}]}
\ \bigoplus_{[(\Gamma,\lambda)]}
C_0\bigl(i\mathfrak{a}_\mathfrak{q}^\ast/W^\sigma(\lambda),\mathfrak{K}\bigr).
\]
<!-- end corollary-1 -->
<!-- blank-1: body_md -->
Let $G$ be a real reductive group in Harish-Chandra's class as in~\cite[Appendix]{Ban05}.
Let $\sigma$ be an involutive automorphism of $G$, and let $H$ be an open subgroup of $G^\sigma$. We say $(G, H)$ is a \emph{reductive symmetric pair},
and call the homogeneous space $X=G/H$ a \emph{reductive symmetric space}. 

For any Lie group~$U$, we shall use the Fraktur letter~$\mathfrak{u}$ for the real Lie algebra of~$U$,
and write  $\mathfrak{u}^{\mathbb{C}}$ or $\mathfrak{u}_\mathbb{C}$ for the complexified Lie algebra.
We shall write $U_0$ for the identity component of~$U$.
<!-- end blank-1 -->
<!-- blank-2: body_md -->
We shall need to fix a convenient maximal compact subgroup of~$G$. In our setting there exists a Cartan involution~$\theta$ of~$G$ that commutes with~$\sigma$  (see \cite[Proposition 1.1]{Ban87-1}); the fixed-point set $K=G^\theta$ is a maximal compact subgroup of~$G$, and has the additional property that $K \cap H = H^\theta$ is a maximal compact subgroup of~$H$. The $K$-homogeneous space $K/(K \cap H)$ is a compact symmetric space\footnote{If $G$ is disconnected, $K$ need not belong to Harish-Chandra's class, but we shall still call $K/K\cap H$ a compact symmetric space when $K$ is compact.}, which will play a role in the paper. 

The involutions $\sigma$ and $\theta$ induce decompositions of the Lie algebra~$\mathfrak{g}$ which are critical to the theory. We have the direct sum decompositions
\[
\mathfrak{g}=\mathfrak{h}\oplus \mathfrak{q},
\qquad
\mathfrak{g}=\mathfrak{k}\oplus \mathfrak{p},
\]
where $\mathfrak{h}$ and $\mathfrak{q}$ are the $(\pm 1)$-eigenspaces of $\sigma$, and $\mathfrak{k}$ and $\mathfrak{p}$ are the $(\pm 1)$-eigenspaces of $\theta$. 

If $\mathfrak{a}$ is a $\sigma$-stable subspace of~$\mathfrak{g}$, we write
\[
\mathfrak{a}_\mathfrak{h}=\mathfrak{a}\cap \mathfrak{h},
\qquad
\mathfrak{a}_\mathfrak{q}=\mathfrak{a}\cap \mathfrak{q},
\]
for the $(\pm 1)$-eigenspaces of~$\sigma$ on~$\mathfrak{a}$, so that $\mathfrak{a} = \mathfrak{a}_\mathfrak{h} \oplus \mathfrak{a}_\mathfrak{q}$. This convention will be used throughout.
<!-- end blank-2 -->
<!-- blank-3: body_md -->
Fix once and for all a nonzero $G$-invariant measure on $X=G/H$. We denote by $\lambda_X$ the left regular representation of~$G$ on~$L^2(X)$. Thus $\lambda_X$ is equivalent to the (normalized, unitary) induction $\mathrm{Ind}_H^G 1_H$, where $1_H$ is the trivial representation of $H$ (see \cite[Appendix E]{BHV}).
<!-- end blank-3 -->
<!-- definition-1: body_md -->
\label{def_Hfixed_dist}
Let $(\pi,V)$ be a unitary representation of $G$.
We denote by $V^\infty$ the Fr\'echet space of smooth vectors, and by $V^{-\infty}$ its strong dual. The action of~$G$ on~$V$ determines an action on~$V^{-\infty}$. An \emph{$H$-fixed distribution vector} for $\pi$ is a continuous linear functional $\eta\in V^{-\infty}$ which is $H$-invariant.
We write
\[
(V^{-\infty})^H
\]
for the space of all such $H$-fixed distributions for $(\pi, V)$.

Suppose $\eta \in (V^{-\infty})^H$. For all $v \in V^\infty$, we let $\eta_v\colon G/H \to \mathbb C$ denote the $C^\infty$ function defined by $\eta_v(gH) = \eta(\pi(g)^{-1}v)$ for all $g \in G$. We define  
\[ m_\eta\colon V^\infty \to C^\infty(G/H)\]
by setting $m_\eta(v)=\eta_v$ for all $v \in V^\infty$.
<!-- end definition-1 -->
<!-- lemma-1: body_md -->
\label{lem_Hdist_embedding}
Let $(\pi,V)$ be an irreducible unitary representation of $G$. The map $\eta \to m_\eta$ defines a linear isomorphism from $ (V^{-\infty})^H$ to the space $\mathrm{Hom}_G(V^\infty, C^\infty(G/H))$ of $G$-equivariant continuous linear maps $V^\infty\to C^\infty(G/H)$. If $\eta\neq 0$, then $m_\eta$ is an embedding.
<!-- end lemma-1 -->
<!-- remark-1: body_md -->
In \cite[p.~14]{Ban_note}, \cite[p.~13]{Ban05}, $H$-fixed distributions ($H$-fixed generalized vectors) are taken to be continuous anti-linear functionals on $V^\infty$.
Passing from a linear functional $\eta$ to the anti-linear functional $v\mapsto \overline{\eta(v)}$ gives an anti-linear isomorphism between the two conventions.
<!-- end remark-1 -->
<!-- definition-2: body_md -->
Let $(G, H)$ be a reductive symmetric pair. The $H$-spherical unitary dual of $G$, denoted by  ${\widehat{G}}_H$, is the subset of the unitary dual $\widehat{G}$ consisting of the equivalence classes of irreducible unitary representations with a nonzero space of $H$-fixed distributions.
<!-- end definition-2 -->
<!-- definition-3: body_md -->
Let $(\pi, V)$ be an irreducible unitary representation of~$G$. We say $\pi$ is \emph{in the discrete series of $X=G/H$} if it is equivalent to an irreducible subrepresentation of the regular representation~$\lambda_X$ of~$G$ on~$L^2(X)$, i.e. if
\[
\mathrm{Hom}_G(V, L^2(X)) \neq0.
\]
We denote by ${\widehat{G}}_{H, \mathrm{ds}}$ the set of equivalence classes of irreducible unitary representations of~$G$ in the discrete series of~$X$;  we say  $X$ \emph{has a discrete series}, or \emph{has discrete series}, when this set is nonempty.
<!-- end definition-3 -->
<!-- definition-4: body_md -->
Let $(\pi, V)$ be an irreducible unitary representation of~$G$ on a Hilbert space~$V$, with space of smooth vectors $V^\infty$.  We call an element $\eta\in (V^{-\infty})^H$  \emph{square-integrable} if there exists $v \in V^\infty\smallsetminus\{0\}$ such that the element~$\eta_v$ of $C^\infty(X)$ (defined in Definition~\ref{def_Hfixed_dist}) is a square-integrable function on~$X$. We denote by $(V^{-\infty})^H_{\mathrm{ds}}$ the vector space of square-integrable $H$-fixed distributions on $V$.
<!-- end definition-4 -->
<!-- lemma-2: body_md -->
\label{lem_sqdis_iff} Let $(\pi, V)$ be an irreducible unitary representation of~$G$, and let $\eta$ be an element of $(V^{-\infty})^H$. 
\begin{enumerate}[(a)]

\item The element $\eta$ is square-integrable if and only if for every $v \in V^\infty$, the function $\eta_v$ is square-integrable on~$X$.
\item Suppose $\eta$ is square-integrable. The map \mbox{$m_\eta\colon V^\infty \to C^\infty(X)$} has image in $C^\infty(X)\cap L^2(X)$ and extends uniquely to a $G$-equivariant continuous map $V \to L^2(X)$.
\end{enumerate}
<!-- end lemma-2 -->
<!-- proof-1: body_md -->
Assertion~(a) immediately follows from~(b): indeed,  if $\eta_v$ is square-integrable on~$X$, then $\eta$ is square-integrable by definition; and if~$m_\eta$ extends uniquely to a $G$-equivariant continuous map $V \to L^2(X)$, then $\eta_v$ is square-integrable for all $v \in V^\infty$. 

Let us prove~(b). The case $\eta=0$ is immediate. Suppose $\eta\neq0$ is square-integrable. Choose $v\in V^\infty\smallsetminus\{0\}$ such that $m_\eta(v)=\eta_v\in C^\infty(X)\cap L^2(X)$. By applying Gårding smoothing $\lambda(f)v = \int_G f(g)\pi(g)vdg$ for some appropriate $f\in C^\infty_c(G)$ and by replacing $v$ with $\lambda(f)v$ if necessary, we may assume that $\eta_v\in L^2(X)^\infty$ (see~\cite[Proposition 3.14]{Knapp}). By projecting $v$ to its nonzero $K$-isotypical component, we can further assume that $v$ is $K$-finite.

Set
\[
M_\eta=m_\eta(V_K)\subset C^\infty(X),
\]
where $V_K$ denotes the space of $K$-finite vectors in~$V$. By
Lemma~\ref{lem_Hdist_embedding}, the map $m_\eta$ is injective; hence
$M_\eta$ is an irreducible $(\mathfrak{g},K)$-module isomorphic to~$V_K$. We have
\[
0\neq \eta_v
\in M_\eta\cap\bigl(L^2(X)^\infty\bigr)_K.
\]
Since
$\bigl(L^2(X)^\infty\bigr)_K$ is a $(\mathfrak{g},K)$-module and $M_\eta$ is
irreducible, the $(\mathfrak{g},K)$-module generated by $\eta_v$ is all of $M_\eta$.
Hence $m_\eta$ restricts to an embedding
\[
m_\eta|_{V_K}\colon V_K\hookrightarrow L^2(X).
\]
Pulling back the $L^2$-inner product along $m_\eta|_{V_K}$ therefore defines a positive-definite invariant Hermitian form on $V_K$.
By uniqueness of invariant Hermitian forms on an irreducible admissible $(\mathfrak{g},K)$-module \cite[proof of Theorem~8]{HC53}, this form is proportional to the one induced from the given Hilbert structure on $V$. Thus, $m_\eta|_{V_K}$ extends to a positive scalar multiple of a $G$-equivariant isometric embedding
\[
V\hookrightarrow L^2(X),
\]
whose restriction to $V^\infty$ coincides with $m_\eta$ by continuity and by density of~$V_K$. Thus $m_\eta(V^\infty)\subset C^\infty(X)\cap L^2(X)$, and $m_\eta$ extends to the embedding $V\to L^2(X)$ above. The uniqueness is clear since $V^\infty$~is dense in~$V$.
<!-- end proof-1 -->
<!-- lemma-3: body_md -->
\label{lem_sq_int_dis} Let $(\pi,V)$ be an irreducible unitary representation of~$G$. For  $\eta \in  (V^{-\infty})^H_{\mathrm{ds}}$, let $\widetilde{m_\eta}$ be the $G$-equivariant map $V \to L^2(X)$ defined in Lemma~\ref{lem_sqdis_iff}(b). The correspondence $\eta\mapsto \widetilde{m_\eta}$ induces a linear isomorphism
    \[
  (V^{-\infty})^H_\mathrm{ds} \simeq  \operatorname{Hom}_G(V, L^2(G/H)).
\]

  In particular, $\pi\in {\widehat{G}}_{H, \mathrm{ds}}$ if and only if $(V^{-\infty})_\mathrm{ds}^H\neq 0$.
<!-- end lemma-3 -->
<!-- proof-2: body_md -->
The injectivity of the map $\eta\mapsto \widetilde{m_\eta}$, $(V^{-\infty})^H_\mathrm{ds} \to  \operatorname{Hom}_G(V, L^2(G/H))$, follows from the fact that the map  $\eta\mapsto m_\eta$ is an isomorphism between $(V^{-\infty})^H $ and $\mathrm{Hom}_G(V^\infty,C^{\infty}(G/H))$ (Lemma~\ref{lem_Hdist_embedding}). 
 
 For $T\in  \operatorname{Hom}_G(V, L^2(G/H))$, the restriction $T|_{V^\infty}$ must be an element of $\mathrm{Hom}_G(V^\infty,C^{\infty}(G/H))$; by Lemma~\ref{lem_Hdist_embedding} it is $m_\eta$ for some $H$-fixed distribution vector $\eta\in (V^{-\infty})^H$. The function $\eta_v=m_\eta(v)=T|_{V^\infty}(v)$ is square-integrable for all $v \in V^\infty$, so $\eta$ is square-integrable by  Lemma~\ref{lem_sqdis_iff}, and $T|_{V^\infty} = m_\eta$. By continuity, this implies $T=\widetilde{m_\eta}$, showing the surjectivity.
<!-- end proof-2 -->
<!-- blank-4: body_md -->
To summarize the above: 
 \emph{an irreducible unitary representation~$\pi$ on~$V$ belongs to ${\widehat{G}}_{H, \mathrm{ds}}$ if and only if $(V^{-\infty})^H_{\mathrm{ds}}\neq 0$.} The multiplicity of $V$ in the discrete series of $L^2(G/H)$ is given by
 \[
 \dim_{\mathbb{C}}(\mathrm{Hom}_G(V, L^2(G/H)))=\dim_{\mathbb{C}}((V^{-\infty})^H_{\mathrm{ds}}).
 \]
Given an embedding $T\colon V\to L^2(G/H)$, the corresponding   $\eta \in (V^{-\infty})^H_\mathrm{ds}$ is obtained by composing $T|_{V^\infty}\colon V^\infty\to L^2(G/H)\cap C^\infty(G/H)$ with the evaluation map  $\delta_{eH}\colon C^\infty(G/H)\to \mathbb{C}$ at the identity coset.
<!-- end blank-4 -->
<!-- blank-5: body_md -->
\emph{Cartan subspaces and the rank condition.}\label{sec:cartan_and_rank} Recall that~$\mathfrak{q}$ denotes the $(-1)$-eigenspace of $\sigma$ on~$\mathfrak{g}$; this vector subspace of $\mathfrak{g}$ can be identified with the tangent space to $G/H$ at $eH$. 
A \emph{Cartan subspace} of $\mathfrak{q}$ is a maximal abelian subspace of~$\mathfrak{q}$ consisting of semisimple elements. Every Cartan subspace of~$\mathfrak{q}$ is conjugate by $H_0$ to a $\theta$-stable Cartan subspace \cite[p.~406, Remark]{OM80}. All Cartan subspaces of $\mathfrak{q}$ have the same dimension; this common dimension is called the (real) \emph{rank} of $X$ and is denoted by
\[
\operatorname{rank}(X)=\operatorname{rank}(G/H).
\]
Since $K/(K \cap H)$ is itself a symmetric space, we may consider the rank  of $K/(K\cap H)$. 
 We say $G/H$  \emph{satisfies the equal-rank condition} if 
 \[
 \operatorname{rank}(G/H) = \operatorname{rank}(K/(K\cap H)).
 \]
 This is equivalent to the existence of a Cartan subspace of $\mathfrak{q}$ which is contained in $\mathfrak{k} \cap \mathfrak{q}$; such a subspace is called a \emph{compact Cartan subspace of~$\mathfrak{q}$} for~$G/H$. If there exists a compact Cartan subspace of $\mathfrak{q}$, then it is unique up to conjugation by $(K\cap H)_0$.
<!-- end blank-5 -->
<!-- theorem-6: body_md -->
\label{thm:equal-rank} The discrete series of a reductive symmetric space $X=G/H$ is nonempty if and only if $X$ satisfies the equal-rank condition.
<!-- end theorem-6 -->
<!-- blank-6: body_md -->
Fix a $\theta$-stable Cartan subspace
$\mathfrak{b}_\mathfrak{q}=\mathfrak{t}_\mathfrak{q}\oplus \mathfrak{a}_\mathfrak{q}$
of $\mathfrak{q}$, where
\[
\mathfrak{t}_\mathfrak{q}=\mathfrak{b}_\mathfrak{q}\cap \mathfrak{k},
\qquad
\mathfrak{a}_\mathfrak{q}=\mathfrak{b}_\mathfrak{q}\cap \mathfrak{p}.
\]
Let $L=Z_G(\mathfrak{a}_\mathfrak{q})$ be the centralizer of $\mathfrak{a}_\mathfrak{q}$ in~$G$. Then $L$ is a $\sigma$-stable and $\theta$-stable Levi subgroup of $G$.
Write $L=MA$ for its Langlands decomposition. The group $M$ is reductive and in Harish-Chandra's class. Since $\mathfrak{t}_\mathfrak{q}\subset \mathfrak{m}\cap \mathfrak{q}$ is a compact Cartan subspace of $\mathfrak{m} \cap \mathfrak{q}$, the smaller symmetric space
\[
M/(M\cap H)
\]
has discrete series by Theorem~\ref{thm:equal-rank}.

Choose a positive system $\Sigma^+(\mathfrak{g},\mathfrak{a}_\mathfrak{q})$ for the restricted root system $\Sigma(\mathfrak{g},\mathfrak{a}_\mathfrak{q})$, and let
\[
\mathfrak{n}=\bigoplus_{\alpha\in \Sigma^+(\mathfrak{g},\mathfrak{a}_\mathfrak{q})} \mathfrak{g}_\alpha.
\]
Then \(\mathfrak{m}\oplus\mathfrak{a}\oplus\mathfrak{n}\) is a \(\sigma\theta\)-stable parabolic subalgebra of \(\mathfrak{g}\) containing \(\mathfrak{b}_\mathfrak{q}\). We define \(P=LN=MAN\), where \(N=\exp(\mathfrak{n})\).

This discussion determines a map 
\begin{equation}\label{sigma_st_parab} \{ (\mathfrak{b}_\mathfrak{q}, \Sigma^+(\mathfrak{g}, \mathfrak{a}_\mathfrak{q}))\} \to \{ \text{parabolic subgroups of~$G$}\},\end{equation}
sending a pair consisting of a $\theta$-stable Cartan subspace of~$\mathfrak{q}$ and a positive system to the corresponding $\sigma\theta$-stable parabolic subgroup $P$.
<!-- end blank-6 -->
<!-- definition-5: body_md -->
A \emph{cuspidal $\sigma$-parabolic subgroup} of $G$ is a parabolic subgroup of~$G$ in the image of~\eqref{sigma_st_parab}. We denote by $\mathcal{P}_{\sigma,\mathrm{cusp}}$ the collection of all cuspidal $\sigma$-parabolic subgroups of $G$.
<!-- end definition-5 -->
<!-- definition-6: body_md -->
Two cuspidal $\sigma$-parabolic subgroups $P_1$, $P_2$ of $G$ are called \emph{$\sigma$-associate} if $(\mathfrak{a}_1)_\mathfrak{q}$ and $(\mathfrak{a}_2)_\mathfrak{q}$ are conjugate by~$K$. We denote by $\mathcal{P}_{\sigma,\mathrm{cusp}}/\!\sim$ the set of $\sigma$-associate classes of cuspidal $\sigma$-parabolic subgroups of $G$.
<!-- end definition-6 -->
<!-- definition-7: body_md -->
\label{def:sigma-principal-series}
Let $P=MAN$ be a cuspidal $\sigma$-parabolic subgroup of $G$. Let $(\xi, V_\xi)$ be a unitary irreducible representation of~$M$ in the discrete series of $M/(M\cap H)$. Let $\nu\in i\mathfrak{a}_\mathfrak{q}^\ast$. Write $e^\nu$ for the unitary character of $A$ given by
$e^\nu(a)=e^{\nu(\log a)}$ for $a\in A$. Here, we regard $\nu$ as a functional on $\mathfrak{a}$ by extending it by zero on $\mathfrak{a}_\mathfrak{h}$. We denote by
\[
\pi_{P,\xi,\nu}
=
\operatorname{Ind}_P^G(\xi\otimes e^\nu\otimes 1)
\]
the $G$-representation obtained by normalized unitary induction from these data. 
We refer to $\pi_{P,\xi,\nu}$ as a \emph{generalized $\sigma$-principal series representation}. We can realize $\pi_{P, \xi, \nu}$ on the space of (a.e. equivalence classes of) measurable functions $f\colon G\to V_\xi$ such that \[
f\mid_K \in L^2(K, V_\xi) \text{ and } f(gman)=e^{-\nu-\rho}(a)\xi(m)^{-1}f(g)
\]
for all $g \in G$ and $man \in MAN$, where $\rho$ is the half-sum of the roots in $\Sigma(\mathfrak{n}, \mathfrak{a})$. The action of~$G$ on such ``functions'' is by left translation and the inner product  of ``functions'' is the $L^2$-inner product between their restrictions to~$K$:
\[
\langle f_1, f_2 \rangle\coloneq \int_{K} \langle f_1(k),  f_2(k) \rangle_{V_\xi}dk.
\]
<!-- end definition-7 -->
<!-- theorem-7: body_md -->
\label{thm_description0}
Let $X=G/H$ be a reductive symmetric space. The subset 
 $\mathrm{supp}(\lambda_X)$ of $\widehat G$ is the closure of $S_X$ in the Fell topology.
<!-- end theorem-7 -->
<!-- proof-3: body_md -->
The Plancherel theorem for reductive symmetric spaces expresses $\lambda_X$ as a direct sum of direct integrals of generalized $\sigma$-principal series representations $\pi_{P,\xi,\nu}$, with $\nu$ ranging over regular elements of $i\mathfrak{a}_\mathfrak{q}^\ast$; see \cite[Theorem~10.9]{BS05-2} and \cite[Theorem~10.15]{Ban05}.
The finite-dimensional multiplicity spaces occurring in those formulas do not affect the support.
Hence $\mathrm{supp}(\lambda_X)$ is the closure of the union of the supports of the corresponding fiber representations.

For the reader's convenience, let us make the connection with the parame-trization of \cite{BS05-2}, in which the discrete-series data are  attached to symmetric spaces of the form
\[
M/(M\cap w^{-1}Hw),
\qquad
w\in W_{K\cap H}\backslash W_K(\mathfrak{a}_\mathfrak{q}^0)/Z_W(\mathfrak{a}_\mathfrak{q}),
\]
where $W_K(\mathfrak{a}_\mathfrak{q}^0)$ is the Weyl group of a fixed maximal abelian subspace $\mathfrak{a}_\mathfrak{q}^0\subset \mathfrak{p} \cap \mathfrak{q}$ containing $\mathfrak{a}_\mathfrak{q}$, $W_{K\cap H}$ is its subgroup generated by the image of the normalizer $N_{K\cap H}(\mathfrak{a}_\mathfrak{q}^0)$  of $\mathfrak{a}_\mathfrak{q}^0$ in $K\cap H$ and $Z_W(\mathfrak{a}_\mathfrak{q})$ is the centralizer of $\mathfrak{a}_\mathfrak{q}$. Conjugation by $w$ identifies this symmetric space with $M^w/(M^w\cap H)$ where $M^w=wMw^{-1}$, transports the discrete-series representation accordingly, and replaces $P$ by a $\sigma$-associate cuspidal $\sigma$-parabolic subgroup attached to $w\mathfrak{a}_\mathfrak{q} w^{-1}\subset \mathfrak{a}_\mathfrak{q}^0$.
Thus the union of irreducible constituents occurring in the Plancherel formula is exactly the union defining $S_X$, except that the Plancherel formula only uses regular parameters.

Since the set of regular elements is dense in $i\mathfrak{a}_\mathfrak{q}^\ast$, and unitary parabolic induction depends continuously on the imaginary parameter in the Fell topology \cite{Fell1962}, allowing all $\nu\in i\mathfrak{a}_\mathfrak{q}^\ast$ changes the union only up to closure. Hence $\mathrm{supp}(\lambda_X)=\overline{S_X}$.
<!-- end proof-3 -->
<!-- theorem-8: body_md -->
\label{thm_description}
Let \(X=G/H\) be a reductive symmetric space.
Then \(S_X\) is a closed subset of \(\widehat G\). Consequently,
\[
\mathrm{supp}(\lambda_X)=S_X\subset \widehat G.
\]
In other words, for any irreducible unitary representation \(\pi\) of \(G\),
\(\pi\) belongs to \(\mathrm{supp}(\lambda_{X})\) if and only if there exist a
cuspidal \(\sigma\)-parabolic subgroup \(P=MAN\) of \(G\), a representation
\(\xi \in {\hat{M}}_{M\cap H, \mathrm{ds}}\) in the discrete series of
\(M/(M\cap H)\), and \(\nu \in i\mathfrak{a}_\mathfrak{q}^*\), such that \(\pi\) is equivalent to an
irreducible constituent of the generalized \(\sigma\)-principal series
representation \(\pi_{P, \xi, \nu}\).
<!-- end theorem-8 -->
<!-- proposition-2: body_md -->
\label{prop_closed_induction} 
 Let $G$ be a real reductive group. 
 Let $P$ be any parabolic subgroup of $G$,
 with Langlands decomposition $P=MAN$. 
 Let $\mathbf{\xi} = (\xi_n)_{n \in \mathbb N}$
 be a sequence  of unitary representations of~$M$.
 Let $\mathbf{Y} = (Y_n)_{n \in \mathbb N}$ be a sequence of closed subsets of $i\mathfrak{a}^\ast$.
 Let $S(P, \mathbf{\xi}, \mathbf{Y})$ be the subset of the unitary dual $\widehat{G}$ consisting of the equivalence classes for all irreducible constituents of the parabolically induced representations $\pi_{P, \xi_n, \nu}$ for $n \in \mathbb N$ and $\nu \in Y_n$. 
 
 If the maximal group $C^\ast$-algebra of~$M$ acts by compact operators in the direct sum representation $\bigoplus_{n \in \mathbb N} \xi_n$, then $S(P, \mathbf{\xi}, \mathbf{Y})$ is a closed subset of $\widehat{G}$.
<!-- end proposition-2 -->
<!-- proof-4: body_md -->
Let $C^*(G)$ be the maximal group $C^*$-algebra of $G$, and $C^*(L)$ be the maximal group $C^*$-algebra of $L=MA$. Let $C^*(G/N)$ be the Hilbert $C^*(G)$-$C^*(L)$ module  introduced in \cite[Section 3.2]{Clare13}, and denoted  $\mathcal{E}(G/N)$ there (see also \cite{CCH16}, where the notation $C^*(G/N)$ comes from). A key property of this module is that $C^*(G)$ acts compactly on $C^*(G/N)$: the proof of \cite[Proposition 4.5]{CCH16} for $C_r^*(G/N)$ works verbatim for $C^*(G/N)$. 
 
 Let $(\xi_n, V_n)_{n \in \mathbb N}$ be a sequence of unitary representations of $M$ such that $C^*(M)$ acts compactly on $V=\bigoplus_n V_n$ through $\xi=\bigoplus_n\xi_n$. Then $C^*(L)$ acts compactly on the $C^*(L)$-$C^*(A)$ module $\mathcal{E} = V \otimes C^*(A)\cong C_0(i\mathfrak{a}^*, V)\cong \bigoplus_n C_0(i\mathfrak{a}^*, V_n)$. By the theory of $C^*$-parabolic induction \cite{Clare13, CCH16}, we have $C^*(G/N)\otimes_{C^*(L)} \mathcal{E} \cong  \bigoplus_n C_0(i\mathfrak{a}^*, \mathrm{Ind}_P^GV_n)$ where, on the fiber at \(\nu\in i\mathfrak{a}^*\), \(G\) acts on
\(\operatorname{Ind}_P^G V_n\) by \(\pi_{P,\xi_n,\nu}\)
\cite[Corollary~3.5]{Clare13}. Moreover, the $C^\ast$-algebra $C^*(G)$ acts on $C^*(G/N)\otimes_{C^*(L)} \mathcal{E}$ compactly.
 
After restriction to the closed subspaces $Y_n\subset i\mathfrak{a}^*$, it follows that the family $\pi_{P, \xi_n, \nu}$ of unitary representations of $G$, for $n\in \mathbb N$ and for $\nu \in Y_n$, induces a $\ast$-homomorphism
\begin{equation}\label{eq-fourier-pi}
\pi\colon C^*(G) \to \bigoplus_{n} C_0(Y_n, \mathfrak{K}(\mathrm{Ind}_P^GV_n)), 
\end{equation}
where $\mathfrak{K}(\mathrm{Ind}_P^GV_n)$ is the $C^*$-algebra of compact operators on the Hilbert space $\mathrm{Ind}_P^GV_n$ of the representation $\pi_{P, \xi_n, \nu}$. Here, the composition of $\pi$ with the evaluation at a point $\nu$ in $Y_n$ gives a representation
\[
 \mathrm{ev}_{\nu} \circ \pi \colon C^*(G) \to  \mathfrak{K}(\mathrm{Ind}_P^GV_n) 
 \]
which is equivalent to the representation of $C^\ast(G)$ on $\mathrm{Ind}_P^GV_n$   induced by the representation $\pi_{P, \xi_n, \nu}$ of $G$. 

Now, let $B$ be the image of $C^\ast(G)$ under~\eqref{eq-fourier-pi}.  Since $B$ is a subalgebra of $\bigoplus_{n} C_0(Y_n, \mathfrak{K}(\mathrm{Ind}_P^GV_n))$, by extension of pure states \cite[Lemma 2.10.1]{Dixmier}, any irreducible representation of $B$ is equivalent to one that factors through the evaluation at some point $\nu$ in $Y_n$. Therefore, the spectrum $\widehat{B}$, which is a closed subspace of $\widehat G$, naturally coincides with the subset $S(P, \{\xi_n\}_n, \{Y_n\}_n)$ of $\hat G$. Hence $S(P, \mathbf{\xi}, \mathbf{Y})$ is closed.
<!-- end proof-4 -->
<!-- corollary-2: body_md -->
\label{cor_closed_induction} Let $G$ be any real reductive group, and let $P=MAN$ be any parabolic subgroup of $G$. Let $\xi \in \hat{M}$ be an irreducible unitary representation of $M$, and let $Y$ be a closed subset of $i\mathfrak{a}^\ast$. The subset $S(P, \xi,Y) \subset \widehat G$, consisting of all the irreducible constituents of the  induced representations $\pi_{P, \xi, \nu}=\operatorname{Ind}^G_{MAN}(\xi\otimes e^{\nu}\otimes 1)$ for $\nu \in Y$, is closed in $\widehat{G}$. In particular, the subset $S(P, \xi) = S(P, \xi, i\mathfrak{a}^\ast)$ is closed in~$\widehat{G}$.
<!-- end corollary-2 -->
<!-- proof-5: body_md -->
By Theorem \ref{thm_description0}, we only need to show that $S_X$ is closed in $\hat G$. We may write $S_X$ as the union of the subsets $S(P, \xi, i\mathfrak{a}_\mathfrak{q}^*)$ defined in Corollary \ref{cor_closed_induction}, as $P$ ranges over cuspidal $\sigma$-parabolic subgroups and $\xi$ ranges over $ \widehat{M}_{M\cap H, \mathrm{ds}}$. By Corollary~\ref{cor_closed_induction}, each subset $S(P, \xi, i\mathfrak{a}_\mathfrak{q}^*)$ is closed. We can say more: for fixed~$P$, the union $S_X(P)=\bigcup_{\xi\in {\hat{M}}_{M\cap H, \mathrm{ds}}} S(P, \xi, i\mathfrak{a}_\mathfrak{q}^*)$ is closed in $\widehat{G}$. This follows from Proposition~\ref{prop_closed_induction} and the uniform admissibility theorem \cite[Proposition 3.1]{BS05-2} (or \cite[Theorem 11.5]{Ban05}). Indeed, the latter directly implies $C^*(K\cap M)$ acts compactly in the representation $\bigoplus_{\xi\in {{\hat{M}}_{M\cap H, \mathrm{ds}}}  }\xi$, and this implies that $C^*(M)$ acts compactly on $\bigoplus_{\xi\in {{\hat{M}}_{M\cap H, \mathrm{ds}}}  }\xi$ by the density of $C^*(M)C^*(K\cap M)$ in $C^*(M)$. Note also that the set ${\hat{M}}_{M\cap H, \mathrm{ds}}$ is countable by the same uniform admissibility.
 
Now let  $\mathcal{P}_0$ be a finite set of cuspidal $\sigma$-parabolic subgroups comprising one per associate class of cuspidal $\sigma$-parabolic subgroups. We have the equality  $S_X=\bigcup_{P \in \mathcal{P}_0}S_X(P)$; therefore $S_X$ is a finite union of closed subsets of~$\widehat{G}$. This implies the theorem.
<!-- end proof-5 -->
<!-- lemma-4: body_md -->
\label{lem:fundamental-cartan-abelian-centralizer}
Under assumption~\eqref{centralizer_compact_cartan}, the Lie algebra
\[
\mathfrak{l}=Z_\mathfrak{g}(\mathfrak{t}_\mathfrak{q})
\]
is a fundamental Cartan subalgebra of $\mathfrak{g}$, that is, a maximally compact Cartan subalgebra. The group centralizer 
\[
L = Z_G(\mathfrak{t}_\mathfrak{q})
\]
is a connected abelian Cartan subgroup of $G$.
<!-- end lemma-4 -->
<!-- proof-6: body_md -->
Because $\mathfrak{t}_\mathfrak{q}\subset \mathfrak{k}$ and $\mathfrak{t}=Z_\mathfrak{k}(\mathfrak{t}_\mathfrak{q})$ is abelian, $\mathfrak{t}$ 
is a Cartan subalgebra of $\mathfrak{k}$ (see \cite[\S\,2, th.~1]{Bourbaki}). Since $\mathfrak{t}\subset \mathfrak{l}$ and since by assumption $\mathfrak{l}$ is abelian, every element of $\mathfrak{l}$ centralizes~$\mathfrak{t}$; hence
\[
\mathfrak{l}\subset Z_\mathfrak{g}(\mathfrak{t}).
\]
The reverse inclusion is immediate from $\mathfrak{t}_\mathfrak{q}\subset \mathfrak{t}$, so $\mathfrak{l}=Z_\mathfrak{g}(\mathfrak{t})$. Now $Z_\mathfrak{g}(\mathfrak{t})$ is the $\theta$-stable Cartan subalgebra of $\mathfrak{g}$ associated with the Cartan subalgebra $\mathfrak{t}$ of $\mathfrak{k}$, so $\mathfrak{l}$ is fundamental.

The group $L=Z_G(\mathfrak{t}_\mathfrak{q})$ has Lie algebra $\mathfrak{l}$. It is connected since $L\cap K = Z_K(\mathfrak{t}_q)$ is connected: the centralizer of any torus in a connected compact Lie group is connected \cite[\S\,2, n°2, cor.~5]{Bourbaki}. Thus, $L\cap K=T=\exp(\mathfrak{t})$ is a maximal torus in $K$. Since \(L\) is \(\theta\)-stable, its Cartan decomposition gives
\(L=(L\cap K)\exp(\mathfrak l\cap\mathfrak p)\). Thus the connectedness of
\(L\cap K\) implies the connectedness of \(L\).  Hence
\[
L=TA
\]
is an abelian Cartan subgroup of $G$ where $T=\exp(\mathfrak{t}) =Z_K(\mathfrak{t}_\mathfrak{q})$ and $A=\exp(\mathfrak{a})$, $\mathfrak{a}=\mathfrak{l}\cap \mathfrak{p}$.
<!-- end proof-6 -->
<!-- blank-7: body_md -->
We fix once and for all a compact Cartan subspace $\mathfrak{t}_\mathfrak{q}$ of $\mathfrak{q}$ satisfying the abelian centralizer condition, and set $\mathfrak{t}\coloneq Z_\mathfrak{k}(\mathfrak{t}_\mathfrak{q})$, $\mathfrak{l}\coloneq Z_\mathfrak{g}(\mathfrak{t}_\mathfrak{q})=Z_\mathfrak{g}(\mathfrak{t})$. Let $L=Z_G(\mathfrak{t}_\mathfrak{q})=TA$ where $T=\exp(\mathfrak{t})$ is a maximal torus in $K$. 

We also fix once and for all a positive system $\Sigma_c^+$ for the root system $\Sigma(\mathfrak{k}^\mathbb{C}, \mathfrak{t}_\mathfrak{q}^\mathbb{C})$, which determines a unique compatible positive system $\Sigma_K^+$ for the root system $\Sigma(\mathfrak{k}^\mathbb{C}, \mathfrak{t}^\mathbb{C})$. Here, the compatibility means that for every $\alpha \in \Sigma^+_K$, the restriction $\alpha\vert_{\mathfrak{t}_\mathfrak{q}}$ is either zero or an element of  $\Sigma^+_c$. In our setting, the restriction is never zero.


 In general, there are finitely many positive systems $\Sigma^+$ for $\Sigma(\mathfrak{g}^\mathbb{C}, \mathfrak{t}_\mathfrak{q}^\mathbb{C})$ that are compatible with the positive system $\Sigma_c^+$ of $\Sigma(\mathfrak{k}^\mathbb{C}, \mathfrak{t}_\mathfrak{q}^\mathbb{C})$. In our setting, such a choice of $\Sigma^+$ determines a unique positive system $\Sigma_G^+$ of $\Sigma(\mathfrak{g}^\mathbb{C}, \mathfrak{t}^\mathbb{C})$ compatible with $\Sigma^+$. Enumerate the positive systems obtained in this way as
\[
\Sigma_{G,1}^+,\dots,\Sigma_{G,m}^+.
\]
This list consists of the systems induced from $\mathfrak{t}_\mathfrak{q}$; it need not exhaust the positive systems of $\Sigma(\mathfrak{g}^\mathbb{C}, \mathfrak{t}^\mathbb{C})$ containing $\Sigma^+_K$.

For each $j \in \{1, \dots, m\}$, define
\[
\mathfrak{u}_j=\bigoplus_{\alpha\in \Sigma_{G,j}^+}\mathfrak{g}_\alpha^{\mathbb C},
\qquad
\mathfrak{q}_j=\mathfrak{l}^{\mathbb C}\oplus \mathfrak{u}_j.
\]
Then $\mathfrak{q}_j$ is a $\theta$-stable Borel subalgebra of $\mathfrak{g}^{\mathbb C}$.
Let
\[
\rho_{G,j}=\frac{1}{2}\sum_{\alpha\in \Sigma_{G,j}^+}\alpha,
\qquad
\rho_{K}=\frac{1}{2}\sum_{\alpha\in \Sigma_{K}^+}\alpha.
\]

\begin{lemma}\label{lem-minus-sigma} We have $\sigma(\rho_K) =-\rho_K$, and $\sigma(\rho_{G,j}) = -\rho_{G,j}$ for all $j \in \{1, \dots m\}$. 
\end{lemma}
\begin{proof}
Under assumption~\eqref{centralizer_compact_cartan}, no root of
\(\Sigma(\mathfrak{g}^\mathbb{C},\mathfrak{t}^\mathbb{C})\) vanishes on \(\mathfrak{t}_\mathfrak{q}\). For each of the compatible
positive systems under consideration, a root \(\alpha\) is positive if and
only if its restriction \(\alpha|_{\mathfrak{t}_\mathfrak{q}}\) is positive. Since \(\sigma\) acts
as \(-1\) on \(\mathfrak{t}_\mathfrak{q}\), we have
\[
(\sigma\alpha)|_{\mathfrak{t}_\mathfrak{q}}=-\alpha|_{\mathfrak{t}_\mathfrak{q}}.
\]
Consequently,
\[
\sigma(\Sigma^+_{G,j})=-\Sigma^+_{G,j},
\qquad
\sigma(\Sigma_K^+)=-\Sigma_K^+,
\]
which implies the result. 
\end{proof}
<!-- end blank-7 -->
<!-- lemma-5: body_md -->
\label{lem-minus-sigma} We have $\sigma(\rho_K) =-\rho_K$, and $\sigma(\rho_{G,j}) = -\rho_{G,j}$ for all $j \in \{1, \dots m\}$.
<!-- end lemma-5 -->
<!-- proof-7: body_md -->
Under assumption~\eqref{centralizer_compact_cartan}, no root of
\(\Sigma(\mathfrak{g}^\mathbb{C},\mathfrak{t}^\mathbb{C})\) vanishes on \(\mathfrak{t}_\mathfrak{q}\). For each of the compatible
positive systems under consideration, a root \(\alpha\) is positive if and
only if its restriction \(\alpha|_{\mathfrak{t}_\mathfrak{q}}\) is positive. Since \(\sigma\) acts
as \(-1\) on \(\mathfrak{t}_\mathfrak{q}\), we have
\[
(\sigma\alpha)|_{\mathfrak{t}_\mathfrak{q}}=-\alpha|_{\mathfrak{t}_\mathfrak{q}}.
\]
Consequently,
\[
\sigma(\Sigma^+_{G,j})=-\Sigma^+_{G,j},
\qquad
\sigma(\Sigma_K^+)=-\Sigma_K^+,
\]
which implies the result.
<!-- end proof-7 -->
<!-- blank-8: body_md -->
Let us introduce  notation related to cohomological induction. Given one of the systems $\Sigma^+_{G, j}$, the elements $2\rho_{G, j}$ and $2\rho_{K}$ are the linear functionals on~$\mathfrak{t}^\mathbb{C}$ determined by the action of~$\mathfrak{l}^\mathbb{C}$ on the top exterior power of $\mathfrak{u}_j$ and $\mathfrak{u}_j\cap \mathfrak{k}^\mathbb{C}$, respectively. To any regular and $\Sigma^+_{G, j}$-dominant~$\lambda\in (\mathfrak{t}_\mathfrak{q}^*)^\mathbb{C}$  such that $\lambda-\rho_{G,j}$ is analytically integral on $T$, we attach a $(\mathfrak{g}, K)$-module $A^{\mathfrak{q}_j}(\lambda)$ by cohomological induction: in the notation of \cite[p.~330, (5.6)]{KnappVogan}, we set 
\[
A^{\mathfrak{q}_j}(\lambda) = \mathcal{R}^{S}_{\mathfrak{q}_j}(\mathbb{C}_{\lambda-\rho_{G,j}})
\]
where  $S=\dim(\mathfrak{u}_j\cap \mathfrak{k}^\mathbb{C})$ and we apply the $\rho$-shift $\lambda-\rho_{G,j}$ to $\lambda$ before applying the Zuckerman functor $\mathcal{R}^{S}_{\mathfrak{q}_j}$.

For fixed $j$ and $\lambda$, set
\begin{equation}\label{eq:mu-lambda}
\mu_\lambda=\lambda+\rho_{G,j}-2\rho_{K}.
\end{equation}

All highest weights for representations of $K$ below are taken with respect to the fixed positive system $\Sigma_K^+$.

With this notation, the description of the discrete series can be summarized as follows when the symmetric space $G/H$ satisfies our condition~\eqref{centralizer_compact_cartan}.
<!-- end blank-8 -->
<!-- theorem-9: body_md -->
\label{thm_Vogan_ds} Let $X=G/H$ be a reductive symmetric space. Suppose $G$ is connected. Assume \eqref{centralizer_compact_cartan}. Let
\[
L^2(X)_d\subset L^2(X)
\]
denote the Hilbert direct sum of the irreducible $G$-subrepresentations of $L^2(X)$. Then the space of $K$-finite vectors of \(L^2(X)_d\) has the
algebraic direct sum decomposition
\[
(L^2(X)_d)_K
\cong
\bigoplus_{j=1}^m\ \bigoplus_{\lambda\in\Lambda_j}
A^{\mathfrak{q}_j}(\lambda),
\]
where $\Lambda_j$ is the set of all $\lambda\in i\mathfrak{t}_\mathfrak{q}^\ast$ such that:
\begin{enumerate}[(i)]
\item $\lambda$ is regular and $\Sigma_{G,j}^+$-dominant;
\item $\mu_\lambda$, as in \eqref{eq:mu-lambda}, is the highest weight of an irreducible $(K \cap H)$-spherical representation of $K$ \textup{(}i.e.\ a representation with a nonzero $K\cap H$-fixed vector\textup{)}. 
\end{enumerate}
<!-- end theorem-9 -->
<!-- theorem-10: body_md -->
\label{thm:Aq-properties} In the setting of Theorem \ref{thm_Vogan_ds}, for any $\lambda \in \Lambda_j$,  
\begin{enumerate}[(a)]
\item $A^{\mathfrak{q}_j}(\lambda)$ is a (nonzero) irreducible $(\mathfrak{g}$-$K$)-module; 
\item $A^{\mathfrak{q}_j}(\lambda)$ has infinitesimal character $\lambda\in (\mathfrak{t}^*)^\mathbb{C} \subset (\mathfrak{l}^*)^\mathbb{C}$ in Harish-Chandra's parametrization;
\item $A^{\mathfrak{q}_j}(\lambda)$ is unitary;
\item $A^{\mathfrak{q}_j}(\lambda)$ is tempered;
\item $A^{\mathfrak{q}_j}(\lambda)$ has a unique lowest $K$-type whose highest weight is $\mu_\lambda$.
\end{enumerate}
<!-- end theorem-10 -->
<!-- proof-8: body_md -->
(a) follows from \cite[Theorem 8.2]{KnappVogan} since $\lambda$ is dominant regular; (b) is the content of \cite[Corollary 5.25 (b)]{KnappVogan}; (c) follows from \cite[Theorem 9.1]{KnappVogan}; (d)  from \cite[Theorem 11.225]{KnappVogan}; (e)  from \cite[Proposition 10.24]{KnappVogan}.
<!-- end proof-8 -->
<!-- definition-8: body_md -->
An irreducible unitary representation of a real reductive Lie group is called \emph{tempiric} if it is tempered and has real infinitesimal character.
<!-- end definition-8 -->
<!-- remark-2: body_md -->
\label{rk-tempiric-regular} For a connected reductive group such as~$G$, every tempiric representation has a unique lowest $K$-type. Suppose $\pi$ is tempiric and has  \emph{regular}  infinitesimal character. Then the space of $K$-finite vectors of $\pi$ is isomorphic to $A^{\mathfrak{q}_0}(\lambda)$ for a $\theta$-stable Borel subalgebra $\mathfrak{q}_0=\mathfrak{l}^\mathbb{C}\oplus \frak u$ where $\Delta^+=\Sigma(\mathfrak{q}_0, \mathfrak{t}^\mathbb{C})$ is compatible with $\Sigma^+_K$, $\lambda\in i\mathfrak{t}^*$ is regular and $\Delta^+$-dominant, and $\lambda-\rho_G$ is analytically integral on $T$. Here  $\rho_G$ denotes the half-sum of the roots in $\Delta^+$, counted with multiplicities. Then the unique lowest $K$-type of $\pi$ has highest weight $\mu =\lambda + \rho_{G} - 2\rho_K$. This follows from \cite[Proposition 10.24, Theorem 11.225]{KnappVogan}.
<!-- end remark-2 -->
<!-- proposition-3: body_md -->
\label{prop_ds_ab}  In the setting of Theorem \ref{thm_Vogan_ds}, the discrete series $\widehat G_{H,\mathrm{ds}}$ of $X=G/H$ is precisely the set of tempiric representations of $G$ which have regular infinitesimal character and whose lowest $K$-type is $K\cap H$-spherical. Each of these representations occurs in $L^2(X)$ with multiplicity one.
<!-- end proposition-3 -->
<!-- proof-9: body_md -->
Suppose first that $[\pi]\in \widehat G_{H,\mathrm{ds}}$. Then the underlying $(\mathfrak{g},K)$-module of $\pi$ occurs in $L^2(X)_d$, so Theorem~\ref{thm_Vogan_ds} yields an index $j$ and a parameter $\lambda\in \Lambda_j$ such that the underlying $(\mathfrak{g},K)$-module of $\pi$ is isomorphic to $A^{\mathfrak{q}_j}(\lambda)$. By Theorem~\ref{thm:Aq-properties}, the representation $\pi$ is tempiric, has regular infinitesimal character, and its unique lowest $K$-type has highest weight $\mu_\lambda$. Condition~(ii) in Theorem~\ref{thm_Vogan_ds} says precisely that this lowest $K$-type is $K\cap H$-spherical.

Conversely, let $\pi$ be a tempiric representation of $G$ with regular infinitesimal character; assume its unique lowest $K$-type is $K\cap H$-spherical. Then $\pi$ is equivalent to $A^{\mathfrak{q}_0}(\lambda)$ for $\mathfrak{q}_0$,  $\lambda \in i\mathfrak{t}^*$, $\Delta^+\supset \Sigma^+_K$, $\rho_G$ as in Remark \ref{rk-tempiric-regular}. The highest weight of its lowest $K$-type is $\mu=\lambda + \rho_G - 2\rho_K$. By the Cartan–Helgason criterion (see Proposition \ref{prop:appendix-connected-CH}), the $K\cap H$-sphericity of $\mu$ implies $\mu \in i\mathfrak{t}_\mathfrak{q}^*$. Since $\rho_K\in i\mathfrak{t}_\mathfrak{q}^*$ by Lemma \ref{lem-minus-sigma}, $\lambda+\rho_G \in i\mathfrak{t}_\mathfrak{q}^*$. Since $\lambda$ is regular and $\Delta^+$-dominant, so is $\lambda +\rho_G$. This implies that $\Delta^+\supset \Sigma^+_K$, which is a positive system determined by $\lambda +\rho_G \in i\mathfrak{t}_\mathfrak{q}^*$, is the one compatible with some positive system $\Sigma^+(\mathfrak{g}^\mathbb{C}, \mathfrak{t}_\mathfrak{q}^\mathbb{C})$ compatible with $\Sigma^+_c$. Hence, $\Delta^+=\Sigma^+_{G, j}$ for some $j$. By Lemma \ref{lem-minus-sigma}, $\rho_G=\rho_{G, j}\in i\mathfrak{t}_\mathfrak{q}^*$. Thus, $\lambda \in i\mathfrak{t}_\mathfrak{q}^*$. The highest weight of its unique lowest $K$-type is $\mu_\lambda$. The sphericity hypothesis is therefore exactly condition~(ii) in Theorem~\ref{thm_Vogan_ds}; hence $[\pi]\in \widehat G_{H,\mathrm{ds}}$.

The lowest-\(K\)-type formula~\eqref{eq:mu-lambda} shows that distinct pairs
\((j,\lambda)\) give different highest weights for the lowest \(K\)-types of
\(A^{\mathfrak{q}_j}(\lambda)\); therefore, these irreducible representations cannot be equivalent.  Hence the decomposition in Theorem~\ref{thm_Vogan_ds} is multiplicity-free, and every representation in $\widehat G_{H,\mathrm{ds}}$ occurs with multiplicity one in $L^2(X)$.
<!-- end proof-9 -->
<!-- proposition-4: body_md -->
\label{prop:ds-distribution-one-dimensional}
In the setting of Theorem \ref{thm_Vogan_ds}, let $(\pi,V)\in \widehat G_{H,\mathrm{ds}}$, and let $\tau_\pi$ be the unique lowest $K$-type of $\pi$. Then $\dim_{\mathbb C}(V^{-\infty})^H_{\mathrm{ds}}=1$, and every nonzero element of $(V^{-\infty})^H_{\mathrm{ds}}$ is nonzero on $\tau_\pi$.
<!-- end proposition-4 -->
<!-- proof-10: body_md -->
By Proposition~\ref{prop_ds_ab}, the representation $\pi$ occurs in $L^2(X)$ with multiplicity one. Hence Lemma~\ref{lem_sq_int_dis} gives $\dim_{\mathbb C}(V^{-\infty})^H_{\mathrm{ds}}=1$.

Suppose $T\colon V\hookrightarrow L^2(X)$ is a $G$-equivariant embedding. Under this embedding, the evaluation functional 
\[
\eta\colon V^\infty\to  L^2(X)\cap C^\infty(X) \to \mathbb C,
\qquad
v\longmapsto (Tv)(eH)
\]
defines a nonzero element of $(V^{-\infty})^H_{\mathrm{ds}}$. Since $(V^{-\infty})^H_{\mathrm{ds}}$ has dimension~1, it is enough to check that $\eta$ is nonzero on $\tau_\pi$ for every such $T$.

Let $(j,\lambda)$ be the unique pair such that the underlying $(\mathfrak{g},K)$-module of $\pi$ is $A^{\mathfrak{q}_j}(\lambda)$. By the work of Flensted-Jensen (see Remark \ref{rem:FJfunc} below), the image $T(V^\infty)$ is explicitly known in our setting. A key point is that the image $T(\tau_\pi)\subset C^\infty(X)$ of the lowest $K$-type contains an explicit vector $\psi_{j,\lambda}$ such that
\[
\psi_{j,\lambda}(eH)\neq 0:
\]
see \cite{FJ80,OM84,S84} and Remark \ref{rem:FJfunc} below. Therefore $\eta$ cannot vanish on~$\tau_\pi$,  proving the assertion.
<!-- end proof-10 -->
<!-- remark-3: body_md -->
\label{rem:FJfunc} Given a pair $(j, \lambda)$ as in Theorem~\ref{thm:Aq-properties}, let us explain how Flensted-Jensen constructs a subrepresentation of $L^2(X)$ equivalent to $A^{\mathfrak{q}_j}(\lambda)$, and how the special function $\psi_{j,\lambda}$ appears. 

Let \(C=H\cap Z(G)\). Since \(C\) is central in \(G\) and contained in \(H\),
the natural identification
\[
G/H\cong (G/C)/(H/C)
\]
also identifies the corresponding regular representations. Moreover, since
\(G\) is connected and reductive, we have \(Z(G/C)=Z(G)/C\), and therefore
\[
(H/C)\cap Z(G/C)=\{e\}.
\]
Thus, after replacing \((G,H)\) by \((G/C,H/C)\), we may assume without loss
of generality that \(H\cap Z(G)=\{e\}\). By splitting off the connected part of the center of $G$ which acts on any irreducible module by a central character, we may assume $G$ is semisimple and this does not affect the assertion $\psi_{j,\lambda}(eH)\neq0$. 

We first treat the case where $H$ is connected. The starting point is the Flensted--Jensen duality (\cite[Theorem 2.3]{FJ80}, \cite[Section 8.2]{S84}):
\begin{equation} \label{eq_FJ_dual}
C_\mu^\infty(G/H) \cong C_{\mu^d}^\infty(G^d/H^d) 
\end{equation}
between the space of $C^\infty$ functions on $X=G/H$ transforming under the $K$-type $\mu$, and the space of $C^\infty$ functions on a ``dual'' symmetric space $X^d = G^d/H^d$, transforming under a certain $K^d$-type $\mu^d$, where $H^d$ is a maximal compact subgroup of $G^d$. 
 As explained in \cite[Proof of Theorem 16.1]{BS05-1}, this holds in our setting where $G$ is not assumed to be linear. 
 Specifically, $G^d, H^d, K^d$ are the analytic subgroups in the complex adjoint group $G_\mathbb{C}$ whose Lie algebras, as subalgebras of $\mathfrak{g}_\mathbb{C}$, are
\[
\mathfrak{g}^d = (\mathfrak{k}\cap \mathfrak{h} \oplus \mathfrak{p}\cap \mathfrak{q}) \oplus i (\mathfrak{k}\cap \mathfrak{q} \oplus \mathfrak{p}\cap \mathfrak{h});
\]
\[
\mathfrak{h}^d = (\mathfrak{k}\cap \mathfrak{h}) \oplus i (\mathfrak{p}\cap \mathfrak{h}), \quad \mathfrak{k}^d = (\mathfrak{k}\cap \mathfrak{h}) \oplus i (\mathfrak{k}\cap \mathfrak{q})
\]
respectively. For any irreducible representation $(\mu, V_\mu)$ of~$K$, $\mu$ extends to an irreducible holomorphic representation of $(K, \mathfrak{k}_\mathbb{C})$. Its restriction to $(K\cap H, \mathfrak{k}^d)$ exponentiates to an irreducible representation $\mu^d$ of $K^d$ with the same highest weight as $\mu$. The duality isomorphism \eqref{eq_FJ_dual} sends
$f\in C^\infty_\mu(G/H)$ to the function $f^d\in C^\infty_{\mu^d}(G^d/H^d)$  defined by
 \[
 f^d(k^d x H^d)\coloneq (\mu^d((k^d)^{-1})f)(xH),
 \]
 for $k^d\in K^d$, $x\in \exp(\mathfrak{p}\cap \mathfrak{q})$. In particular, we have
 \begin{equation} \label{eq_FJ_dual_e}
 f(eH) = f^d(eH^d).
 \end{equation}
See \cite[Section 8.2]{S84}.

 
 Now let $\lambda$ be an element of $\Lambda_j$ as in Theorem \ref{thm_Vogan_ds}, and let $\mu$ be an irreducible representation of $K$ whose highest weight is the functional $\mu_\lambda$ in~\eqref{eq:mu-lambda}. Let \(\psi_{j,\lambda}\in C^\infty_\mu(G/H)\) be the function corresponding, under the isomorphism~\eqref{eq_FJ_dual}, to the function \(\psi^d_{j,\lambda}\in C^\infty_{\mu^d}(G^d/H^d)\) given by
 \[
 \psi_{j, \lambda}^d(xH^d) = \int_{K\cap H}e^{\langle-\lambda -\rho_{G,j}, t^d(x^{-1}k)\rangle}dk
 \]
 where $t^d$ in the exponent is the projection from $G^d=H^d \cdot \exp{i \mathfrak{t}_\mathfrak{q}} \cdot N^d$ (the Iwasawa decomposition) to $T^d= \exp{i \mathfrak{t}_\mathfrak{q}}$ followed by the logarithm map (see  \cite[Remark 2]{OM84}, \cite[Section 8.3]{S84}). Then  $\psi_{j,\lambda}$ is square-integrable on $X=G/H$ (\cite{FJ80}, \cite{OM84}, \cite[Theorem 8.3.1]{S84}).  It is clear that $\psi^d_{j,\lambda}(eH^d)>0$ and hence $\psi_{j,\lambda}(eH)>0$ by \eqref{eq_FJ_dual_e}. Flensted--Jensen proves that the closed \(G\)-subrepresentation of \(L^2(X)\) generated by \(\psi_{j,\lambda}\) is an irreducible discrete-series representation \cite{FJ80}. Under Vogan's 
parametrization in terms of cohomological induction \cite[Theorem~2.9]{V88}, its underlying \((\mathfrak{g},K)\)-module is
\(A^{\mathfrak{q}_j}(\lambda)\). By definition   $\psi_{j,\lambda}$ lies in the $\mu$-isotypical subspace of $A^{\mathfrak{q}_j}(\lambda)$, where $\mu$ is the unique lowest $K$-type of  $A^{\mathfrak{q}_j}(\lambda)$. This completes our discussion of the Flensted-Jensen construction when $H$ is connected.

For disconnected \(H\), pullback along \(G/H_0\to G/H\) identifies
\(L^2(G/H)\) with the \(H/H_0\)-fixed subspace of \(L^2(G/H_0)\).
The corresponding orthogonal projection is the normalized averaging operator
\[
(Pf)(gH_0)
=
\frac{1}{[H:H_0]}
\sum_{hH_0\in H/H_0} f(ghH_0).
\]
If an irreducible representation \(\pi\) occurs in \(L^2(G/H)\), then \(P\)
is nonzero on the corresponding discrete summand of \(L^2(G/H_0)\).
By the connected-case multiplicity-one statement and Schur's lemma, \(P\)
acts as the identity on that summand. Hence its Flensted--Jensen function is
\(H/H_0\)-invariant and descends to \(G/H\), while its nonzero value at the
identity coset is unchanged.
<!-- end remark-3 -->
<!-- lemma-6: body_md -->
\label{lem:welltemp-all-cartan}
Let $(G, H)$ be a reductive symmetric pair. The following conditions are equivalent:
\begin{enumerate}[(1)]
\item There exists a Cartan subspace $\mathfrak{b}_\mathfrak{q}\subset \mathfrak{q}$ such that the Lie algebra centralizer $Z_\mathfrak{g}(\mathfrak{b}_\mathfrak{q})$ is abelian.
\item For every Cartan subspace $\mathfrak{b}_\mathfrak{q}\subset \mathfrak{q}$, 
the centralizer $Z_\mathfrak{g}(\mathfrak{b}_\mathfrak{q})$ is abelian.
\item For every Cartan subspace $\mathfrak{b}_{\mathfrak{q}^\mathbb{C}} \subset \mathfrak{q}^\mathbb{C}$ of $\mathfrak{q}^\mathbb{C}$, the centralizer $Z_{\mathfrak{g}^\mathbb{C}}(\mathfrak{b}_{\mathfrak{q}^\mathbb{C}})$ is abelian.
\end{enumerate}
<!-- end lemma-6 -->
<!-- proof-11: body_md -->
That (3) implies (2) follows from the fact that  $Z_{\mathfrak{g}^{\mathbb C}}({\mathfrak{b}_\mathfrak{q}}^{\mathbb C})=Z_\mathfrak{g}({\mathfrak{b}_\mathfrak{q}})^{\mathbb C}$ for every Cartan subspace $\mathfrak{b}_\mathfrak{q} \subset \mathfrak{q}$. That (2) implies (1) is immediate. 
 
Let us prove that (1) implies (3).  By the Kostant--Rallis conjugacy theorem \cite[Theorem 1]{KostantRallis1971} for complex reductive symmetric
pairs, all Cartan subspaces of \(\mathfrak q^\mathbb C\) are conjugate under
the identity component of the fixed-point group in the complexified pair.
Therefore the ${\mathfrak g}^{\mathbb \mathbb C}$-centralizers of all Cartan subspaces of $\mathfrak q^\mathbb C$ are conjugate. Given a Cartan subspace $\mathfrak{b}_\mathfrak{q} \subset \mathfrak{q}$, one  of the centralizers of the previous sentence is 
\[
Z_{\mathfrak g^\mathbb C}(\mathfrak b_{\mathfrak q}^\mathbb C)
=
Z_{\mathfrak g}(\mathfrak b_{\mathfrak q})^\mathbb C;
\]
if this one is abelian, all of them are abelian.
<!-- end proof-11 -->
<!-- definition-9: body_md -->
\label{def_welltemp}
The reductive symmetric space $X=G/H$ is called \emph{well-tempered} if the equivalent conditions in Lemma \ref{lem:welltemp-all-cartan} hold.
<!-- end definition-9 -->
<!-- lemma-7: body_md -->
\label{lem:welltemp_hereditary}
Assume that $X=G/H$ is well-tempered.
Let
\[
\mathfrak{b}_\mathfrak{q}=\mathfrak{t}_\mathfrak{q}\oplus \mathfrak{a}_\mathfrak{q}
\]
be a $\theta$-stable Cartan subspace of $\mathfrak{q}$ such that $Z_\mathfrak{g}(\mathfrak{b}_\mathfrak{q})$ is abelian, and let
\[
L=Z_G(\mathfrak{a}_\mathfrak{q})=MA
\]
be the associated Levi subgroup.
The symmetric space
\[
M/(M\cap H)
\]
is again well-tempered.
<!-- end lemma-7 -->
<!-- proof-12: body_md -->
The subspace $\mathfrak{t}_\mathfrak{q}$ is a Cartan subspace of $\mathfrak{m}\cap \mathfrak{q}$. Indeed, if \(\mathfrak c\subseteq\mathfrak m\cap\mathfrak q\) were a Cartan
subspace properly containing \(\mathfrak t_{\mathfrak q}\), then
\(\mathfrak c\oplus\mathfrak a_{\mathfrak q}\) would be an abelian subspace of
semisimple elements in \(\mathfrak q\) properly containing
\(\mathfrak b_{\mathfrak q}\), contradicting the maximality of
\(\mathfrak b_{\mathfrak q}\).  Since $\mathfrak{m}\subset Z_\mathfrak{g}(\mathfrak{a}_\mathfrak{q})$, we obtain 
\[
Z_\mathfrak{m}(\mathfrak{t}_\mathfrak{q})=\mathfrak{m}\cap Z_\mathfrak{g}(\mathfrak{t}_\mathfrak{q})\subset Z_\mathfrak{g}(\mathfrak{a}_\mathfrak{q})\cap Z_\mathfrak{g}(\mathfrak{t}_\mathfrak{q})=Z_\mathfrak{g}(\mathfrak{b}_\mathfrak{q}).
\]
The Lie algebra $Z_\mathfrak{g}(\mathfrak{b}_\mathfrak{q})$ is abelian by assumption, hence so is $Z_\mathfrak{m}(\mathfrak{t}_\mathfrak{q})$.
Therefore $M/(M\cap H)$ is well-tempered.
<!-- end proof-12 -->
<!-- remark-4: body_md -->
Lemma~\ref{lem:welltemp_hereditary} is the basic permanence statement needed later. Combining it with Theorem~\ref{thm_description} and the concrete descriptions
of the discrete series for the smaller symmetric spaces, as in Section~\ref{sec:dis} above and Section~\ref{sec:disc-welltemp} below, we shall see that the tempered spectrum of well-tempered symmetric spaces can be described in simple terms.
<!-- end remark-4 -->
<!-- definition-10: body_md -->
A $G$-homogeneous space $X$ is called \emph{$G$-tempered}, or simply \emph{tempered}, if the regular representation $\lambda_{X}$ of~$G$ on~$L^2(X)$ is weakly contained in the regular representation $\lambda_G$ of~$G$ on~$L^2(G)$; in other words, if every irreducible representation in the support of~$\lambda_{X}$ is tempered as a representation of~$G$.
<!-- end definition-10 -->
<!-- proposition-5: body_md -->
\label{prop:equiv-welltemp} Let $(G, H)$ be a reductive symmetric pair. The following conditions are equivalent:
\begin{enumerate}
\item\label{item-1} $G/H$ is well-tempered.
\item\label{item-2} There is an element in $\mathfrak q$ that is regular semisimple as an
element of \(\mathfrak g\);
\item\label{item-3} The set
\[
\{x \in \mathfrak{q} \mid  \text{$x$ is regular semisimple as an element of $\mathfrak{g}$} \}
\]
is dense in $\mathfrak{q}$ in the Euclidean topology.
\item\label{item-4} The set
\[
S=\{x \in \mathfrak{q} \mid  \text{$Z_\mathfrak{h}(x)$ is abelian} \}
\]
is dense in $\mathfrak{q}$ in the Euclidean topology.
\end{enumerate}
<!-- end proposition-5 -->
<!-- proof-13: body_md -->
\eqref{item-1} \(\implies\) \eqref{item-2}:
Let \(\mathfrak{b}_\mathfrak{q}\subset\mathfrak{q}\) be a Cartan subspace and put
\[
\mathfrak{b}=Z_\mathfrak{g}(\mathfrak{b}_\mathfrak{q}).
\]
By assumption, \(\mathfrak{b}\) is abelian. Since \(\mathfrak{b}_\mathfrak{q}\subset\mathfrak{b}\), we have
\[
\mathfrak{b}=Z_\mathfrak{g}(\mathfrak{b}_\mathfrak{q})\supseteq Z_\mathfrak{g}(\mathfrak{b})\supseteq\mathfrak{b},
\]
and hence \(Z_\mathfrak{g}(\mathfrak{b})=\mathfrak{b}\). Moreover, \(\mathfrak{b}\) is reductive, since it is
the centralizer of a subspace of semisimple elements. Thus \(\mathfrak{b}\) is a Cartan subalgebra of \(\mathfrak{g}\).

No root in \(\Sigma(\mathfrak{g}^\mathbb{C},\mathfrak{b}^\mathbb{C})\) vanishes identically on \(\mathfrak{b}_\mathfrak{q}\):
otherwise the corresponding root space would be contained in
\(Z_{\mathfrak{g}^\mathbb{C}}(\mathfrak{b}_\mathfrak{q}^\mathbb{C})=\mathfrak{b}^\mathbb{C}\). We may therefore choose
\(x\in\mathfrak{b}_\mathfrak{q}\) such that
\[
\alpha(x)\neq0
\qquad
\text{for every }\alpha\in\Sigma(\mathfrak{g}^\mathbb{C},\mathfrak{b}^\mathbb{C}).
\]
Then \(x\) is a regular semisimple element of \(\mathfrak{g}\) contained in \(\mathfrak{q}\).

\eqref{item-2} \(\implies\) \eqref{item-3}:
The set of regular semisimple elements of \(\mathfrak{g}\) is Zariski open.
Its intersection with \(\mathfrak{q}\) is nonempty by assumption and is therefore
Zariski open dense, hence Euclidean open dense, in \(\mathfrak{q}\).

\eqref{item-3} \(\implies\) \eqref{item-4}:
If \(x\in\mathfrak{q}\) is regular semisimple as an element of \(\mathfrak{g}\), then
\(Z_\mathfrak{g}(x)\) is an abelian Cartan subalgebra. Since it is
\(\sigma\)-stable, it decomposes as
\[
Z_\mathfrak{g}(x)=Z_\mathfrak{h}(x)\oplus Z_\mathfrak{q}(x).
\]
In particular, \(Z_\mathfrak{h}(x)\) is abelian, so \(S\) contains every
\(\mathfrak{g}\)-regular semisimple element of \(\mathfrak{q}\). Condition~\eqref{item-3}
therefore implies that \(S\) is dense in \(\mathfrak{q}\).

\eqref{item-4} \(\implies\) \eqref{item-1}:
Let \(\mathfrak{q}^{ss,\mathrm{reg}}\) denote the set of semisimple elements of
\(\mathfrak{q}\) that are regular for the symmetric pair \((\mathfrak{g},\mathfrak{h})\), equivalently
those semisimple \(x\) for which \(\dim Z_\mathfrak{q}(x)\) is minimal. This set is
open and dense in \(\mathfrak{q}\); see \cite[Theorem~5 and the preceding
discussion]{vanDijk}. Since \(S\) is dense and
\(\mathfrak{q}^{ss,\mathrm{reg}}\) is nonempty and open, we may choose
\[
x\in S\cap\mathfrak{q}^{ss,\mathrm{reg}}.
\]
Set
\[
\mathfrak{b}_\mathfrak{q}=Z_\mathfrak{q}(x).
\]
Then \(\mathfrak{b}_\mathfrak{q}\) is a Cartan subspace of \(\mathfrak{q}\). Relative to \(\mathfrak{b}_\mathfrak{q}\),
regularity means that \(\alpha(x)\neq0\) for every nonzero restricted root
\(\alpha\). The restricted-root decomposition therefore gives
\[
Z_\mathfrak{g}(x)=Z_\mathfrak{g}(\mathfrak{b}_\mathfrak{q})
       =Z_\mathfrak{h}(\mathfrak{b}_\mathfrak{q})\oplus\mathfrak{b}_\mathfrak{q}.
\]
In particular, \(Z_\mathfrak{h}(x)=Z_\mathfrak{h}(\mathfrak{b}_\mathfrak{q})\). Since \(x\in S\),
\(Z_\mathfrak{h}(x)\) is abelian. The subspace \(\mathfrak{b}_\mathfrak{q}\) is also abelian, and
\(Z_\mathfrak{h}(\mathfrak{b}_\mathfrak{q})\) centralizes it. Hence \(Z_\mathfrak{g}(\mathfrak{b}_\mathfrak{q})\) is abelian, proving
that \(G/H\) is well-tempered.
<!-- end proof-13 -->
<!-- theorem-11: body_md -->
\label{prop:complex-temp-welltemp}
Let $G/H$ be a complex symmetric space.
Then $G/H$ is tempered if and only if it is well-tempered.
<!-- end theorem-11 -->
<!-- proof-14: body_md -->
By \cite[Corollary~8.6]{BK21}, which is a consequence of \cite[Theorem~1.6 and criterion (1.1)]{BK21}, for complex semisimple algebraic \(G\) and
complex reductive~\(H\), temperedness of \(L^2(G/H)\) is equivalent to the
density of points in \(\mathfrak q\) with abelian stabilizer in \(\mathfrak h\).
For a complex symmetric space, this is condition~(4) of
Proposition~\ref{prop:equiv-welltemp}, hence it is equivalent to
well-temperedness.
<!-- end proof-14 -->
<!-- remark-5: body_md -->
Suppose $G/H$ is a complex symmetric space,  and let $G_{\mathbb R}$ and $H_\mathbb R$ be the fixed points in $G$ and $H$ of an antiholomorphic involution of~$G$ commuting with~$\sigma$, so that we may form the real symmetric space $G_\mathbb R/H_\mathbb R$. Then it is a consequence of Lemma~\ref{lem:welltemp-all-cartan} that $G_{\mathbb R}/H_\mathbb R$ is well-tempered if and only if $G/H$ is well-tempered. Taking into account Theorem~\ref{prop:complex-temp-welltemp}, we see that \emph{$G_{\mathbb R}/H_\mathbb R$ is well-tempered if and only if $G/H$ is tempered}.
<!-- end remark-5 -->
<!-- theorem-12: body_md -->
\label{thm:temp-welltemp}
Let $G/H$ be a symmetric space where $G$ is a real semisimple algebraic group and $H$ is a real reductive algebraic subgroup. If $G/H$ is well-tempered, then $G/H$ is tempered.
<!-- end theorem-12 -->
<!-- proof-15: body_md -->
Suppose $G/H$ is well-tempered. By Proposition \ref{prop:equiv-welltemp}, regular semisimple elements are dense in $\mathfrak{q}$, and for any such $x\in \mathfrak{q}$, $Z_H(x)$ is real reductive algebraic and \(Z_\mathfrak{h}(x)\) is abelian. Hence the identity component
\(Z_H(x)_0\) is abelian and has finite index in \(Z_H(x)\), so
\(Z_H(x)\) is virtually abelian, meaning that it contains an abelian
subgroup of finite index \cite[p.~834]{BK21}.

It follows that elements $x$ in $\mathfrak{q}$ such that $Z_H(x)$ is virtually abelian are dense in $\mathfrak{q}$. By \cite[Theorem~1.1 (2)]{BK21}, this implies $G/H$ is tempered.
<!-- end proof-15 -->
<!-- remark-6: body_md -->
The algebraic hypotheses in Theorem~\ref{thm:temp-welltemp} are those of
\cite{BK21}. For more general reductive symmetric spaces, the fact that well-temperedness implies temperedness also follows
from the Plancherel theorem together with the description of the discrete series of well-tempered symmetric spaces. We shall omit the details.
<!-- end remark-6 -->
<!-- example-1: body_md -->
\label{ex:GcGr-welltemp}
Let $G$ be a connected complex reductive Lie group, regarded as a real Lie group, and let $H$ be an open subgroup of a real form of $G$.
Then $G/H$ is well-tempered.
<!-- end example-1 -->
<!-- proof-16: body_md -->
Write $\mathfrak{g}=\mathfrak{h}\oplus i\mathfrak{h}$ as real Lie algebras, so $\mathfrak{q}=i\mathfrak{h}$. Let $\mathfrak{b}_\mathfrak{h}\subset \mathfrak{h}$ be a Cartan subalgebra of $\mathfrak{h}$. Then $\mathfrak{b}_\mathfrak{q}=i\mathfrak{b}_\mathfrak{h}\subset \mathfrak{q}$ is a Cartan subspace of $\mathfrak{q}$. Since the complexification $\mathfrak{b}_\mathfrak{h}^{\mathbb C}=\mathfrak{b}_\mathfrak{h} \oplus i\mathfrak{b}_\mathfrak{h} $ is a Cartan subalgebra of $\mathfrak{g}$, the space $\mathfrak{b}_\mathfrak{h}^{\mathbb C}$ is its own  centralizer in $\mathfrak{g}$. 
Hence $Z_\mathfrak{g}(\mathfrak{b}_\mathfrak{q})=\mathfrak{b}_\mathfrak{h}\oplus i\mathfrak{b}_\mathfrak{h}$ is abelian.
<!-- end proof-16 -->
<!-- example-2: body_md -->
\label{ex:GmodK-welltemp}
Let $G$ be a connected semisimple Lie group with finite center, and let $K$ be a maximal compact subgroup of~$G$. The Riemannian symmetric space $G/K$ is well-tempered if and only if $G$ is quasi-split.
<!-- end example-2 -->
<!-- proof-17: body_md -->
Let $\theta$ be an involution of~$G$ with fixed-point set $K$, and let $\mathfrak{p}$ be the $(-1)$-eigenspace of $\theta$ on $\mathfrak{g}$. A Cartan subspace of $\mathfrak{q}=\mathfrak{p}$ is exactly a maximal abelian subspace $\mathfrak{a}\subset \mathfrak{p}$. Hence, $G/K$ is well-tempered if and only if $Z_\mathfrak{g}(\mathfrak{a})$ is abelian. For a connected semisimple real Lie group, this occurs if and only if $G$ is quasi-split.
<!-- end proof-17 -->
<!-- example-3: body_md -->
\label{ex:GcKc-welltemp}
Let $G_1$ be a connected real semisimple Lie group with maximal compact subgroup $K_1$. Let $G=G_{1,\mathbb{C}}$, and let $H=K_{1,\mathbb{C}}$.
Then the complex symmetric space $G/H = G_{1,\mathbb C}/K_{1,\mathbb C}$ is well-tempered if and only if $G_1$ is quasi-split.
<!-- end example-3 -->
<!-- proof-18: body_md -->
The complex symmetric space $G_{1,\mathbb C}/K_{1,\mathbb C}$ is well-tempered if and only if the real form $G_{1}/K_1$ is well-tempered: this follows from Lemma \ref{lem:welltemp-all-cartan}. As in Example \ref{ex:GmodK-welltemp}, $G_{1}/K_1$ is well-tempered exactly when $G_1$ is quasi-split.
<!-- end proof-18 -->
<!-- example-4: body_md -->
\label{ex:quaternionic-exception} Let $\mathbb{H}$ denote the field of quaternions. 
For every $m\geq 2$, the symmetric space
\[
\mathrm{SL}(2m-1,\mathbb H)\big/S\bigl(\mathrm{GL}(m,\mathbb H)\times \mathrm{GL}(m-1,\mathbb H)\bigr)
\]
is tempered but not well-tempered.
<!-- end example-4 -->
<!-- proof-19: body_md -->
See \cite[Section~8.5(2)]{BK21} for the temperedness. To see that the
space is not well-tempered, let \(e_{r,s}\) denote the standard quaternionic
matrix unit and fix an imaginary quaternion
\(\mathbf i\in\mathbb H\) with \(\mathbf i^2=-1\).
A Cartan subspace \(\mathfrak{b}_\mathfrak{q}\subset\mathfrak{q}\) is spanned over \(\mathbb{R}\) by
\[
e_{r,m+r}+e_{m+r,r},
\qquad
\mathbf i(e_{r,m+r}+e_{m+r,r}),
\qquad 1\leq r\leq m-1.
\]
Its centralizer contains the nonabelian Lie subalgebra
\[
(\operatorname{Im}\mathbb H)e_{m,m}\cong\mathfrak{sp}(1),
\]
and therefore is not abelian.
<!-- end proof-19 -->
<!-- theorem-13: body_md -->
Let $(G, H)$ be a symmetric pair. Suppose $\mathfrak{g}$ is a real simple Lie algebra and $\mathfrak{h}$ is a semisimple Lie subalgebra whose adjoint group has no compact factor. Assume $\mathfrak{g}$ is isomorphic  neither to $\mathfrak{e}_{6(-26)}$ nor to $\mathfrak{e}_{6(-14)}$. Then $G/H$ is tempered if and only if one of the following holds:
\begin{enumerate}
\item $G/H$ is well-tempered; 
\item $(\mathfrak{g}, \mathfrak{h}) \cong (\mathfrak{sl}(2m-1,\mathbb{H}),\ \mathfrak{sl}(m, \mathbb{H}) \oplus \mathfrak{sl}(m-1,\mathbb{H}))$ for some $ m \geq 2$.
\end{enumerate}
<!-- end theorem-13 -->
<!-- examples-1: body_md -->
\label{example_welltempered_classical}~
\begin{itemize}
    \item Let $p_1, p_2, q_1, q_2 \geq1$. The symmetric space \[
\mathrm{SO}(p_1+p_2,q_1+q_2)/
\bigl(\mathrm{SO}(p_1,q_1)\times \mathrm{SO}(p_2,q_2)\bigr)
\]
is tempered if and only if 
    \[
    \left|p_1+q_1-p_2-q_2\right| \leq 2;
    \]
    In that case it is well-tempered.
    \item The symmetric space
    $\mathrm{SL}(m+n, \mathbb R) / \mathrm{S}(\mathrm{GL}(m, \mathbb R) \times \mathrm{GL}(n, \mathbb R))$ is tempered if and only if $|m-n| \leq 1$; in that case it is well-tempered.
    \item The symmetric space $\mathrm{SO}(m+n, \mathbb{C})/ \mathrm{SO}(m, \mathbb{C}) \times \mathrm{SO}(n, \mathbb{C})$ is tempered if and only if $|m-n| \leq 2$; in that case it is well-tempered.
    \item The space $\mathrm{SL}(p+q, \mathbb{R}) / \mathrm{SO}(p, q)$ is well-tempered for any $p,q$.
\end{itemize}
<!-- end examples-1 -->
<!-- blank-9: body_md -->
For more examples of tempered homogeneous spaces, we refer the reader to \cite{BK15,BK21, BK22}. For classical symmetric spaces $X$ satisfying the equal-rank condition, Mœglin and Renard \cite[Table 1]{Moeglin_Renard} have explicit computations of the centralizer $\mathfrak{l}_X$ of a compact Cartan subspace. In that table, we can easily read off which spaces $X$ are well-tempered: they are well-tempered precisely when $\mathfrak{l}_X$ is abelian. For example, $\mathrm{Sp}(2n, \mathbb{R})/\mathrm{GL}(n, \mathbb{R})$ is an equal-rank well-tempered symmetric space for any $n\geq1$.
<!-- end blank-9 -->
<!-- definition-11: body_md -->
\label{def-character-datum-G} A  \emph{tempered character datum for \(G\)} is a quadruple
\[
(TA,\Gamma,\lambda,\nu),
\]
where \(TA\) is a \(\theta\)-stable Cartan subgroup as above,
\(\Gamma\) is a character of \(T\), \(\lambda\in i\mathfrak{t}^\ast\) is
\(M\)-regular, \(\nu\in i\mathfrak{a}^\ast\), and
\[
d\Gamma=\lambda+\rho_{\mathfrak{m}}-2\rho_{\mathfrak{m}\cap\mathfrak{k}}
\qquad\text{in }i\mathfrak{t}^\ast.
\]
<!-- end definition-11 -->
<!-- lemma-8: body_md -->
\label{lem:rho-rho-eq}
Let \((TA,\Gamma,\lambda,\nu)\) be a tempered character datum for \(G\). Suppose that \(\lambda\) is \(G\)-regular, i.e.\
\[
\langle\alpha,\lambda\rangle\neq0
\qquad
\text{for every }\alpha\in\Sigma(\mathfrak{g}^\mathbb{C},\mathfrak{b}^\mathbb{C}).
\]
Let \(\Sigma^+(\mathfrak{g}^\mathbb{C},\mathfrak{b}^\mathbb{C})\) be the unique positive system for which
\(\lambda\) is dominant, and let \(\Sigma^+(\mathfrak{k}^\mathbb{C},\mathfrak{t}^\mathbb{C})\) be the induced compact positive system. Let \(\rho_G\) and \(\rho_K\) be the corresponding
half-sums of positive roots. Then
\[
\rho_{\mathfrak{m}}-2\rho_{\mathfrak{m}\cap\mathfrak{k}}
=
\rho_G-2\rho_K
\]
in \(i\mathfrak{t}^\ast\).
<!-- end lemma-8 -->
<!-- proof-20: body_md -->
Since \(\lambda\) is \(G\)-regular, no root of
\((\mathfrak{g}^\mathbb{C},\mathfrak{b}^\mathbb{C})\) has zero pairing with \(\lambda\). We may
write a root of \((\mathfrak{g}^\mathbb{C},\mathfrak{b}^\mathbb{C})\) as \((\alpha,\beta)\in
(\mathfrak{t}^\ast\oplus\mathfrak{a}^\ast)^\mathbb{C}\). Then
\[
\mathfrak{g}^\mathbb{C}
=
\mathfrak{m}^\mathbb{C}\oplus
\bigoplus_{(\alpha,\beta),\,\beta\neq0}\mathfrak{g}^\mathbb{C}_{\alpha,\beta},
\qquad
\mathfrak{m}^\mathbb{C}
=
\mathfrak{b}^\mathbb{C}\oplus
\bigoplus_{(\alpha,0),\,\alpha\neq0}\mathfrak{g}^\mathbb{C}_{\alpha,0}.
\]
The positive roots are determined by the sign of
\(\langle\alpha,\lambda\rangle\). We show that
\begin{equation}\label{eq:rho-difference}
\rho_G-\rho_{\mathfrak{m}}
=
2(\rho_K-\rho_{\mathfrak{m}\cap\mathfrak{k}}).
\end{equation}
The Cartan involution~\(\theta\) acts by the identity on \(\mathfrak{t}\) and by minus the
identity on \(\mathfrak{a}\), and hence sends a root
\((\alpha,\beta)\) to \((\alpha,-\beta)\). Since positivity is determined
by \(\langle\alpha,\lambda\rangle\), the two roots in this pair are
simultaneously positive or simultaneously negative.

For each positive pair with \(\beta\neq0\), its contribution to
\(\rho_G-\rho_{\mathfrak{m}}\), regarded as a functional on \(\mathfrak{t}^\mathbb{C}\), is
\[
\frac12\bigl((\alpha,\beta)+(\alpha,-\beta)\bigr)
 \big|_{\mathfrak{t}^\mathbb{C}}
=
\alpha.
\]
Moreover, \(\theta\) interchanges the two root spaces
\(\mathfrak{g}^\mathbb{C}_{\alpha,\beta}\) and
\(\mathfrak{g}^\mathbb{C}_{\alpha,-\beta}\). Their direct sum therefore decomposes into
one-dimensional \(+1\)- and \(-1\)-eigenspaces of~\(\theta\), both of
\(\mathfrak{t}^\mathbb{C}\)-weight \(\alpha\), lying respectively in \(\mathfrak{k}^\mathbb{C}\) and
\(\mathfrak{p}^\mathbb{C}\). Thus the same pair contributes
\(\frac12\alpha\) to \(\rho_K-\rho_{\mathfrak{m}\cap\mathfrak{k}}\). Summing over all
positive pairs proves \eqref{eq:rho-difference}, and rearranging this
identity proves the lemma.
<!-- end proof-20 -->
<!-- definition-12: body_md -->
\label{def-rep-associated-to-chardatum} Given a tempered character datum $(TA, \Gamma, \lambda, \nu)$ for~\(G\),
we denote by
\[
\Phi_G(TA,\Gamma,\lambda,\nu)\subset\widehat G_{\mathrm{temp}}
\]
the (finite) subset of $\widehat{G}$ consisting of the (equivalence classes of the) irreducible constituents of
\(X_G(TA,\Gamma,\lambda,\nu)\). It is a subset of $\widehat{G}_{\mathrm{temp}}$, the tempered dual of~$G$.
<!-- end definition-12 -->
<!-- remark-7: body_md -->
There is an obvious action of $K$ on the set of all tempered character data for~$G$, and on the set of discrete character data. We denote by \[
[TA,\Gamma,\lambda,\nu].
\]
the $K$-conjugacy class of a character datum \((TA, \Gamma, \lambda, \nu)\), and by \([TA,\Gamma,\lambda]\) the $K$-conjugacy class of a discrete character datum. In Definition~\ref{def-rep-associated-to-chardatum}, the set \(X_G(TA,\Gamma,\lambda,\nu)\) depends only on the $K$-conjugacy class $[TA,\Gamma,\lambda,\nu]$.
<!-- end remark-7 -->
<!-- notation-1: body_md -->
\label{notation-w} Given a character datum $(TA, \Gamma, \lambda, \nu)$,
set \begin{align*}
&W(\mathfrak{t}\oplus\mathfrak{a}) =N_K(\mathfrak{t}\oplus\mathfrak{a})/Z_K(\mathfrak{t}\oplus\mathfrak{a}),
\\
& W(\lambda)=\{w\in W(\mathfrak{t}\oplus\mathfrak{a}):w\lambda=\lambda\}, \text{ and}\\
& W(\Gamma,\lambda)=\{w\in W(\lambda):w\Gamma=\Gamma\}.
\end{align*}
Let \(\mathcal C_G\) denote the set of \(K\)-conjugacy classes
\([TA,\Gamma,\lambda]\) of discrete character data for \(G\).
<!-- end notation-1 -->
<!-- theorem-14: body_md -->
~
\label{thm:HC_disjoint}
\begin{enumerate}[(a)]
\item Given a discrete character datum $(TA, \Gamma, \lambda)$, the set  $\Phi_G(TA,\Gamma,\lambda,\nu)$ depends only on the equivalence class of $\nu$ in $i\mathfrak{a}^\ast/W(\Gamma,\lambda)$.
\item
The tempered dual of~\(G\) partitions as 
\[
\widehat G_{\mathrm{temp}}
=
\bigsqcup_{[TA,\Gamma,\lambda,\nu]}
\Phi_G(TA,\Gamma,\lambda,\nu)
=
\bigsqcup_{[TA,\Gamma,\lambda]\in\mathcal C_G}
\bigsqcup_{\nu\in i\mathfrak{a}^\ast/W(\Gamma,\lambda)}
\Phi_G(TA,\Gamma,\lambda,\nu).
\]
\item Given a character datum $(TA, \Gamma, \lambda, \nu)$, all elements of $\Phi_G(TA,\Gamma,\lambda,\nu)$ have the same image in the universal Hausdorff quotient $\widehat G_{\mathrm{temp},\mathrm{Haus}}$. Sending a character datum $(TA, \Gamma, \lambda, \nu)$ to the image of  $\Phi_G(TA,\Gamma,\lambda,\nu)$  in $\widehat{G}_{\mathrm{temp},\mathrm{Haus}}$ yields an identification 
\[
\widehat G_{\mathrm{temp},\mathrm{Haus}}
\cong
\bigsqcup_{[TA,\Gamma,\lambda]\in\mathcal C_G}
 i\mathfrak{a}^\ast/W(\Gamma,\lambda).
\]
\end{enumerate}
<!-- end theorem-14 -->
<!-- proof-21: body_md -->
The first two assertions are Vogan's parametrization of tempered irreducible representations by
character data; see \cite[Section~6.6]{Voganbook}. The description of the
Hausdorff quotient follows from the same parametrization together with standard remarks on the connection between parabolic induction and the Fell topology. One way to obtain it is through
the \(C^\ast\)-algebraic realization of parabolic induction and the separation of the components of \(\widehat G_{\mathrm{temp},\mathrm{Haus}}\) by lowest \(K\)-types, as in \cite{CHS24, CHST24}.
<!-- end proof-21 -->
<!-- lemma-9: body_md -->
\label{lem:G-regular-standard-irreducible}
Let \((TA,\Gamma,\lambda,0)\) be a character datum for \(G\), and suppose
that \(\lambda\) is \(G\)-regular. Then
\[
X_G(TA,\Gamma,\lambda,0)
\]
is irreducible. It has a unique lowest \(K\)-type \((\tau, V)\). Relative to the positive
system $\Sigma^+_K=\Sigma^+(\mathfrak{k}^\mathbb{C}, \mathfrak{t}^\mathbb{C})$ for which \(\lambda\) is dominant, the highest-weight representation $(\mu, V^\mathfrak{n})$ of $T^l=N_K(\mathfrak{t}, \Sigma^+_K)$ attached to $\tau$ contains the \(T\)-character \(\Gamma\). Moreover, the highest-weight representation  $(\mu, V^\mathfrak{n})$ is equivalent to the induced representation $\mathrm{Ind}_T^{T^l}\Gamma$.
<!-- end lemma-9 -->
<!-- proof-22: body_md -->
By definition, the representation $X_G(TA,\Gamma,\lambda,0)$ is a finite direct sum of tempiric representations. Now \cite[Thm.~6.5.9]{Voganbook} describes a specific subset $A(\mathfrak{q},\delta)\subset \widehat{K}$ of the lowest $K$-types of $X_G(TA,\Gamma,\lambda,0)$. Each element of $A(\mathfrak{q},\delta)$ occurs with multiplicity one in $X_G(TA,\Gamma,\lambda,0)$. Furthermore, every irreducible submodule of $X_G(TA,\Gamma,\lambda,0)$ contains some $\tau\in A(\mathfrak{q},\delta)$. Here, $\delta=\Gamma \otimes \Lambda^{\dim(\mathfrak u \cap \mathfrak{p}^\mathbb{C}) }(\mathfrak u \cap \mathfrak{p}^\mathbb{C})^\ast\in \widehat{T}$ where $\mathfrak u$ is the nil-radical of the relevant $\theta$-stable parabolic subalgebra of $\mathfrak{g}^\mathbb{C}$ as in \cite[Convention~6.6.3]{Voganbook}. Vogan also describes a bijection between  $A(\mathfrak{q},\delta)$ and a finite set  $A_L(\delta)\subset \widehat{L\cap K}=\widehat{T}$, defined in \cite[Definition 4.3.15]{Voganbook}: see \cite[Definition~6.5.5]{Voganbook} for the correspondence. In our case, where $L=TA$ is a Cartan subgroup, running through the definitions reveals that $A_L(\delta)=\{\delta\}$. Together, these facts imply that $X_G(TA,\Gamma,\lambda,0)$ is irreducible, hence tempiric, and has a unique lowest $K$-type $\tau$. The correspondence \cite[Definition~6.5.5]{Voganbook} says that $\tau$ has highest weight $d\Gamma=d\delta + 2\rho_{\mathfrak u \cap \mathfrak{p}^\mathbb{C}}$ and $\tau\mid_T$ contains $\Gamma = \delta \otimes \Lambda^{\dim(\mathfrak u \cap \mathfrak{p}^\mathbb{C}) }(\mathfrak u \cap \mathfrak{p}^\mathbb{C})$. These facts imply that the highest-weight representation of $T^l$ attached to $\tau$ contains the $T$-character~$\Gamma$.

We show that the irreducible representation $(\mu, V^\mathfrak{n})$ of $T^l$ is equivalent to the induced representation $\mathrm{Ind}_T^{T^l}\Gamma$. We show this by proving $\mathrm{Ind}_T^{T^l}\Gamma$ is irreducible. If $n \in T^l$ stabilizes $\Gamma \in \widehat{T}$, it must fix $d\Gamma = \lambda +\rho_G-2\rho_K$. Because $G$ is in Harish-Chandra's class and $\lambda$ is $G$-regular, the action of $n$ on $\mathfrak{t}_{\mathbb C}\oplus \mathfrak{a}_\mathbb{C}$ is represented by a Weyl group element $w \in W_G$ that preserves $\Sigma_K^+$. Thus, we have $w\cdot \rho_K = \rho_K$ and $w\cdot d\Gamma = d\Gamma$. Hence, $w\cdot (\lambda +\rho_G) =\lambda + \rho_G$. Since $\lambda$ is $G$-regular and dominant, $\lambda + \rho_G$ is $G$-regular. The freeness of the Weyl action on regular elements yields $w=1$, forcing $n \in Z_K(\mathfrak{t}) = T$. Therefore, the stabilizer of \(\Gamma\) in \(T^l\) is exactly \(T\). It follows $\mathrm{Ind}_T^{T^l}\Gamma$ is irreducible. Consequently, $(\mu, V^\mathfrak{n})$ is equivalent to $\mathrm{Ind}_T^{T^l}\Gamma$.
<!-- end proof-22 -->
<!-- theorem--1: body_md -->
\label{thm:ds_para}
Let \(X=G/H\) be a well-tempered symmetric space. Suppose that \(G\) is a
real reductive linear group in Vogan's class and that \(X\) has discrete
series. For an irreducible unitary representation \((\pi,V)\) of \(G\), the
following conditions are equivalent:
\begin{enumerate}[(1)]
\item \(\pi\) belongs to the discrete series of~$X$; 
\item \(\pi\) is tempiric with regular infinitesimal character, and its unique 
lowest \(K\)-type~\(\tau_\pi\) satisfies
\[
\tau_\pi^{K\cap H}\neq0;
\]
\item \(\pi\) is equivalent to the irreducible representation
\[
X_G(TA,\Gamma,\lambda,0)
\]
for a discrete character datum based on the fundamental Cartan subgroup
\(TA=Z_G(\mathfrak{l})\), where \(\lambda\in i\mathfrak{t}_\mathfrak{q}^\ast\) is \(G\)-regular and, after
replacing the datum by an equivalent \(T^l\)-conjugate if necessary, the character~$\Gamma$ satisfies
\[
\Gamma|_{T\cap H}=1.
\]
\end{enumerate}
Moreover, for any \((\pi,V)\) satisfying these equivalent conditions, we have
\[
\dim_\mathbb{C} (V^{-\infty})^H_{\mathrm{ds}}
=
\dim_\mathbb{C} \tau_\pi^{K\cap H}.
\]
<!-- end theorem--1 -->
<!-- proof-23: body_md -->
We first prove the equivalence of (1) and (2), together with the dimension
formula. If \(G\) and \(H\) are connected, this is exactly
Proposition~\ref{prop_ds_ab} together with Proposition~\ref{prop:ds-distribution-one-dimensional} and Proposition~\ref{prop:appendix-connected-CH}. For the general case considered here, we inspect what happens upon restriction to the identity components. The restriction of \(V\) to \(G_0\) is a finite direct sum of irreducible
representations in the discrete series of $G_0/H_0$, so the assertion that $(\pi,V)$ is tempiric and has regular infinitesimal character follows directly from Proposition~\ref{prop_ds_ab}. By Lemma ~\ref{lem:G-regular-standard-irreducible}, $\pi$ has unique lowest $K$-type $\tau_\pi$. Applying
Proposition~\ref{prop:ds-distribution-one-dimensional} to each summand for the connected
symmetric space \(G_0/H_0\) gives an $K\cap H$-equivariant isomorphism
\[
(V^{-\infty})^{H_0}_{\mathrm{ds}}
\cong
(\tau_\pi^\ast)^{K\cap H_0}.
\]
by restriction of linear functionals to the
lowest \(K_0\)-types, where the star denotes contragredient and the
right-hand side is understood after restricting~\(\tau_\pi\) to $K_0\supset (K\cap H)_0 = K\cap H_0$.
Since \(H/H_0\) is finite and \(H=H_0(K\cap H)\), taking invariants gives
\[
(V^{-\infty})^H_{\mathrm{ds}}
=\bigl((V^{-\infty})^{H_0}_{\mathrm{ds}}\bigr)^{K\cap H}
\cong
\bigl((\tau_\pi^\ast)^{K\cap H_0}\bigr)^{K\cap H}
=
(\tau_\pi^\ast)^{K\cap H}.
\]
Thus \((V^{-\infty})^H_{\mathrm{ds}}\neq0\) if and only if
\(\tau_\pi^{K\cap H}\neq0\), and the displayed dimension formula follows.
